docs.title: HitStor
docs.text:
Encrypted, deduplicated backups for Windows and Linux — server, agents and web dashboard.

Quick start Download What's new

HitStor backs up files and applications on your Windows and Linux machines to a repository you control — a local disk or any S3-compatible bucket. A central server schedules the work, agents on each machine do the backups and restores, and a web dashboard lets your team run everything from a browser. Data is deduplicated across every machine, compressed with Zstd and encrypted with AES-256-GCM before it is written.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Encrypted and deduplicated

    FastCDC chunking (256 KiB–4 MiB), deduplication across hosts, Zstd compression and AES-256-GCM. Local and S3-compatible repositories.

    How it works

  • Server and agents

    One server, agents on Linux (amd64, arm64) and Windows that run as services, talk gRPC over TLS and only send new data.

    Deploy agents

  • Scheduled, verified backups

    Cron schedules with time zones, consistent snapshots (VSS, LVM, btrfs), and an automatic restore check after each backup.

    Backup jobs

  • Restores and disaster recovery

    Browse snapshots, restore files anywhere, or rebuild a whole host with the guided disaster recovery wizard.

    Restore

  • SQL Server and plugins

    Signed workload plugins installed per agent. The SQL Server plugin does full, differential and log backups through VDI, with point-in-time restore.

    SQL Server

  • Users, roles and audit

    Accounts with roles per agent, mandatory two-step verification, and a tamper-evident audit log.

    Users and access

  • PDF reports by email

    Protection summaries and daily status reports, emailed on a schedule through SMTP or Microsoft 365.

    Reports

  • Easy to install

    Windows installers, .deb/.rpm packages, self-extracting Linux installers and a Docker image. Dashboard in English and Spanish.

    Installation

docs.title: Administration Guide
docs.text:
The HitStor Administration Guide is for system administrators responsible for deploying, configuring, and maintaining HitStor backup infrastructure. It covers server setup, agent management, TLS configuration, monitoring, and security hardening.

If you are looking for instructions on creating and restoring backups, see the User Guide instead.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text: Guide Description Server Setup Initialize a repository, start the server, configure systemd, and manage firewall rules. TLS Certificates Configure auto-generated or custom TLS certificates for gRPC and dashboard communication. Backup Jobs Filesystem and workload backup jobs, backup plans, scheduling, and retention. Agent Management Register, configure, and remove backup agents. Agent Discovery Network scan for unregistered agents. Agent Deployment Install and configure the hitstor-agent binary on Linux and Windows machines. Dashboard Access the web dashboard, its pages, and the JSON API. Users and Access Accounts, roles, two-step verification, email, and the audit log. Reports PDF reports emailed on a schedule or downloaded. Server Settings Central settings hub: TLS, network, integrations (Gemini), notifications, email, plugin packages. Monitoring Prometheus metrics, webhook alerting, and Grafana integration. Scheduling Configure server-managed schedules, daemon mode, and systemd timers. Sentinel Ransomware telemetry and alerts. Security Encryption model, key derivation, API key management, and systemd hardening. Troubleshooting Common errors, diagnostic commands, and log analysis. Roadmap Current priorities and out-of-scope surfaces.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Before following the guides in this section, make sure you have HitStor installed. See the Installation Guide for platform-specific instructions.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
Throughout the Administration Guide the following conventions are used:

  • Commands prefixed with $ are run in a terminal.
  • Text in UPPER_CASE (such as AGENT_NAME) represents a value you must replace with your own.
  • Optional flags are shown in square brackets: [--flag VALUE].
  • Long commands are split across multiple lines with \ for readability.
  • Configuration file paths assume a standard Linux installation. Adjust paths for other platforms as needed.

docs.title: Agent Deployment
docs.text: This guide covers installing and configuring the hitstor-agent binary on Linux and Windows machines.

docs.title: Install with the .run Installer (Recommended)
docs.text:
The .run installer includes an interactive wizard that configures the agent and starts the service automatically:

sudo ./hitstor-agent-X.Y.Z-linux-amd64.run

The wizard asks for one value, the listen port (gRPC port the server uses to manage the agent; default 8422). It then installs the binary and the systemd units, writes /etc/hitstor/agent.env, starts the hitstor-agent service, and displays the agent token with instructions for adding the agent from the dashboard. No server address or API key is needed at install time: the server sends them when you register the agent.

docs.title: Non-Interactive Install
docs.text:
For automation, use --no-wizard; the only setting is the listen port:

sudo HITSTOR_AGENT_LISTEN_PORT=8422 \
     ./hitstor-agent-X.Y.Z-linux-amd64.run --no-wizard

See Linux Quick Install for full details.

docs.title: Install from Package
docs.text:
Alternatively, install the agent from a deb or rpm package:

# Debian / Ubuntu
sudo apt install ./hitstor-agent_X.Y.Z_amd64.deb

# RHEL / Fedora / AlmaLinux
sudo rpm -i hitstor-agent-X.Y.Z-1.x86_64.rpm

The package does not start the agent. Enable it with sudo systemctl enable --now hitstor-agent; the token is generated on the first start. See Installation for additional installation methods.

docs.title: Dashboard-Managed Agent (Recommended)
docs.text:
The agent reads its listen port from /etc/hitstor/agent.env:

# /etc/hitstor/agent.env
HITSTOR_AGENT_LISTEN_PORT=8422

When the server registers the agent from the dashboard, the agent rewrites this file with the server address and API key (HITSTOR_AGENT_SERVER, HITSTOR_AGENT_API_KEY). The agent token is stored at /etc/hitstor/agent-token.

To view the agent token:

sudo hitstor-agent show-id

docs.title: Manual (CLI) Registration
docs.text:
If you registered the agent on the server with hitstor serve agent add <name>, put the server address and the printed API key in /etc/hitstor/agent.env yourself, then restart the service:

# /etc/hitstor/agent.env
HITSTOR_AGENT_SERVER=backup.example.com:8420
HITSTOR_AGENT_API_KEY=a3f8c1d9e4b7...6f2a0e5d

Set file permissions so only root can read the key:

sudo chmod 0600 /etc/hitstor/agent.env
sudo chown root:root /etc/hitstor/agent.env

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
Variable Description HITSTOR_AGENT_LISTEN_PORT gRPC listen port for dashboard management (default: 8422) HITSTOR_AGENT_SERVER Server address in host:port format (written at registration) HITSTOR_AGENT_API_KEY 64-character hex API key (written at registration) HITSTOR_AGENT_CA_CERT Path to CA certificate for TLS verification (optional; without it the agent pins the server certificate on first use)

The daemon and the Windows service read agent.env themselves; one-off commands such as hitstor-agent ping or backup read these variables from the environment, from --server/--api-key/--ca-cert, or from agent_server/agent_api_key/agent_ca_cert in the file given with --config.

docs.title: Retrieve the Agent Token
docs.text:
Dashboard-managed agents generate a token on their first start. To display it:

sudo hitstor-agent show-id

The token is stored at /etc/hitstor/agent-token with mode 0600.

docs.title: Test the Connection
docs.text:
Once the agent is registered, verify it can reach the server (the variables come from agent.env):

sudo sh -c 'set -a; . /etc/hitstor/agent.env; hitstor-agent ping'

Expected output:

Server: backup.example.com:8420
Version: X.Y.Z
Repo ID: 03b9cb33...

If this fails, see Troubleshooting for common connection issues.

docs.title: Run a Manual Backup
docs.text:
Create a backup of one or more directories:

sudo sh -c 'set -a; . /etc/hitstor/agent.env; hitstor-agent backup /etc /home /var/lib'

The agent sends the data to the server over gRPC. Progress is displayed in the terminal.

docs.title: Daemon Mode
docs.text:
In daemon mode, the agent runs continuously with two functions:

  1. Management server — listens on port 8422 for gRPC commands from the HitStor server (registration, filesystem and plugin browsing, plugin installation, restores, wake-up)
  2. Backup polling — polls the server for its backup schedule and executes backups automatically
hitstor-agent daemon

If the agent is not yet registered, the daemon waits for registration from the dashboard, then runs the backup jobs created for it.

docs.title: Systemd Integration
docs.text: The agent package includes two systemd units:

docs.title: Daemon Mode (Recommended)
docs.text:
Enable the persistent daemon service:

sudo systemctl enable hitstor-agent
sudo systemctl start hitstor-agent

This starts hitstor-agent daemon as a long-running service. The agent listens for management commands and polls the server for schedule updates.

docs.title: Timer Unit
docs.text: Versions before 0.2.1 shipped a hitstor-agent.timer that only started the daemon again; packages and installers now remove it, since the server schedules every backup. For OS-scheduled one-shot backups, see Scheduling → systemd Timer (alternative).

docs.title: Check Agent Status
docs.text:
sudo systemctl status hitstor-agent
sudo journalctl -u hitstor-agent -f

docs.title: Install the Agent
docs.text:
Download the Windows agent installer (hitstor-agent-X.Y.Z-windows-amd64-setup.exe) from the HitStor releases page and run it as an administrator. The installer:

  • Asks for the listen port (default 8422)
  • Installs hitstor-agent.exe and adds its folder to the system PATH
  • Writes C:\ProgramData\HitStor\agent.env and agent-config.yaml, readable only by SYSTEM and Administrators
  • Adds a Windows Firewall rule for the listen port
  • Registers and starts the HitStorAgent Windows Service ("HitStor Backup Agent"), which runs the daemon
  • Shows the agent token

Then add the agent from the dashboard (Agents → + Add Agent) with its IP address and token. See Windows Agent Installation.

docs.title: Configure the Agent
docs.text:
Registration from the dashboard writes the server address and API key to C:\ProgramData\HitStor\agent.env, which the service reads. For an agent registered with hitstor serve agent add, write that file yourself:

# C:\ProgramData\HitStor\agent.env
HITSTOR_AGENT_SERVER=backup.example.com:8420
HITSTOR_AGENT_API_KEY=a3f8c1d9e4b7...6f2a0e5d
# Optional: CA certificate for TLS verification
# HITSTOR_AGENT_CA_CERT=C:\ProgramData\HitStor\ca.crt

Then restart the service (hitstor-agent service stop, hitstor-agent service start).

docs.title: Test the Connection
docs.text:
Open an elevated PowerShell window and pass the server and key (the command line does not read agent.env):

hitstor-agent ping --server backup.example.com:8420 --api-key KEY

docs.title: Run a Manual Backup
docs.text: hitstor-agent backup --server backup.example.com:8420 --api-key KEY C:\Users C:\Data

docs.title: Manage the Windows Service
docs.text:
The installer registers the service. To manage it by hand:

hitstor-agent service install
hitstor-agent service start
hitstor-agent service stop
hitstor-agent service uninstall

You can also manage the service through the Windows Services console (services.msc).

docs.title: Deploying to Multiple Machines
docs.text:
For large-scale deployments, use configuration management tools (Ansible, Puppet, Chef, or similar) to:

  1. Install the hitstor-agent package and enable the hitstor-agent service
  2. The agent automatically generates a token on first start
  3. Collect agent tokens (via hitstor-agent show-id) and add agents from the dashboard
  4. Create backup jobs for them in the dashboard (Backups → + New Backup Job)

Alternatively, for legacy deployments:

  1. Register each agent with hitstor serve agent add on the server
  2. Deploy /etc/hitstor/agent.env with the server address and the machine-specific API key
  3. Deploy the CA certificate file if you do not want the agent to pin the server certificate on first use (see TLS Certificates)
  4. Enable and start the hitstor-agent systemd service

docs.text:
• Agent Management — add agents from the dashboard or CLI
  • Scheduling — configure backup schedules for deployed agents
  • Monitoring — set up alerts for agent health
  • Troubleshooting — resolve connection and backup issues

docs.title: Agent Auto-Discovery
docs.text: The dashboard can discover hitstor-agent instances on your local network without manually entering every hostname.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
1. Open Agents in the dashboard and click + Add Agent (administrators)
  2. Stay on the Network Scan tab
  3. Select one of the server's subnets (from /api/discover/subnets)
  4. Click Scan Network — the server probes port 8422 on every address of the subnet (up to a /16; the scan stops after 30 seconds) and shows the agents found with their host name, OS, version, and whether they are already registered
  5. Click Register on an agent, enter its name and token, and click Register Agent

docs.title: Manual Entry
docs.text:
Use Manual Entry for a single machine: type the agent's IP address and click Connect. The server probes that address on port 8422 and, if an agent answers, offers to register it.

Discovery and manual entry only use port 8422. For an agent on another port, or behind NAT, register it through the API with its full address: POST /api/agents with name, agent_addr (host:port) and token (see Dashboard → JSON API).

docs.title: API
docs.text: Method Path Description GET /api/discover/subnets List the server's IPv4 subnets POST /api/discover/scan Scan a subnet ({"cidr": "..."}, IPv4, /16 or smaller); returns an operation ID whose progress streams from /api/operations/{id}/events POST /api/discover/probe Probe a specific IP address

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Agents must run in daemon mode with AgentService listening (default port 8422)
  • Server must reach agent addresses on the network (firewall rules)
  • After discovery, complete registration with the agent's token (hitstor-agent show-id); the server then sends the agent its API key. What to back up is chosen afterwards in a backup job

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Agent Management
  • Agent Deployment

docs.title: Agent Management
docs.text: HitStor supports two methods for registering backup agents: dashboard-managed (recommended) and CLI-based (legacy). Dashboard-managed agents use a token-based flow where the server connects to the agent, authenticates, and auto-configures it. CLI-based agents use a manually-distributed API key.

docs.title: Dashboard-Managed Agents (Recommended)
docs.text: Dashboard-managed agents are added directly from the web dashboard. The server connects to the agent over gRPC, authenticates using the agent's token, and sends it the API key and server address automatically.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
1. Install the agent on the remote machine (see Agent Deployment)
  2. The agent generates a token on its first start — note the token (hitstor-agent show-id) and the machine's IP address
  3. Ensure port 8422 (agent gRPC listen port) is reachable from the server

docs.title: Add an Agent from the Dashboard
docs.text:
1. Open the HitStor dashboard at https://SERVER_IP:8421 (administrators)
  2. Navigate to Agents and click + Add Agent
  3. Choose Network Scan to scan a local subnet, or Manual Entry to type the agent's IP address and click Connect
  4. Click Register on the agent found, and fill in Register Agent:
    • Agent Name — descriptive identifier (for example, web-server-01); letters, numbers, hyphens, and underscores
    • Agent Address — host:port, filled in from the scan (for example, 192.168.1.50:8422)
    • Agent Token — 64-character hex token from the agent (hitstor-agent show-id on the agent machine)
  5. Click Register Agent

See Agent Discovery for the network scan workflow.

The server connects to the agent, verifies the token, and sends an API key and the server address, which the agent writes to its agent.env. No manual key copy is needed. Registering again with an existing name re-registers that agent (new API key) and keeps its jobs.

docs.title: Choose What to Back Up
docs.text: What an agent backs up is set per backup job, not on the agent. In Backups → + New Backup Job, the selection tree browses the agent's filesystem (and its installed plugins) live over gRPC; check the folders to back up. See Backup Jobs.

docs.title: Remove an Agent
docs.text:
From the Agents list or the agent's page (Remove, administrators), or via the CLI:

hitstor serve agent remove AGENT_NAME

This revokes the agent's API key. The agent can no longer connect to the server. Existing snapshots created by the agent are not deleted. The dashboard asks whether to keep the agent's backup jobs; the CLI deletes them unless you add --keep-jobs.

docs.title: CLI-Based Agents (Legacy)
docs.text: CLI-based agents are registered from the server command line. The API key must be manually copied to the agent machine.

docs.title: Register an Agent
docs.text:
hitstor serve agent add AGENT_NAME

On success, the command prints a 64-character hexadecimal API key:

Agent "web-server-01" registered.
API Key: a3f8c1d9e4b7...6f2a0e5d

Save this key — it cannot be displayed again.

Copy this key to the agent's /etc/hitstor/agent.env file as HITSTOR_AGENT_API_KEY, next to HITSTOR_AGENT_SERVER (see Agent Deployment).

docs.title: List Agents
docs.text:
View all registered agents (both managed and CLI-based):

hitstor serve agent list

Output:

NAME                  CREATED               LAST BACKUP           MANAGED   SUSPENDED   ADDR
web-server-01         2026-02-01 10:12:40   2026-02-21 03:00:12   yes       no          192.168.1.50:8422
db-primary            2026-02-01 10:20:05   2026-02-21 03:15:08   no        no          -
staging-app           2026-02-03 09:41:17   never                 yes       yes         192.168.1.52:8422

--all-repos lists the agents of every configured repository; --json prints the records as JSON.

docs.title: Remove an Agent
docs.text:
hitstor serve agent remove AGENT_NAME

To keep the agent's backup jobs (for example, to register it again under the same name):

hitstor serve agent remove AGENT_NAME --keep-jobs

Removing an agent never deletes its snapshots; use hitstor forget for that.

docs.title: Agent Status
docs.text:
The dashboard's Agents page shows each agent's status:

Status Meaning ok Agent has backed up within the stale threshold (alert_stale_threshold, default 25 hours) stale Agent has not backed up within the stale threshold never Agent is registered but has never completed a backup suspended Agent is suspended (by an operator or by Sentinel); it cannot back up

The dashboard, the Prometheus metrics and the webhook alerts all use the same alert_stale_threshold; see Monitoring.

docs.title: Agent Token (Dashboard-Managed)
docs.text:
Dashboard-managed agents authenticate using a token — a 64-character hexadecimal string (256 bits of entropy) generated on the agent's first start (the installers start the agent, so it exists right after installation).

Token properties:

  • Generated automatically on the agent's first start, stored at /etc/hitstor/agent-token (mode 0600; C:\ProgramData\HitStor\agent-token on Windows)
  • Retrievable any time with sudo hitstor-agent show-id
  • Stored encrypted (AES-256-GCM) on the server in the agent registry
  • Used by the server to authenticate gRPC calls to the agent (registration, browsing, plugin installation, wake-up)

docs.title: API Key Security (CLI-Based)
docs.text:
CLI-based agents authenticate to the server using a 64-character hexadecimal API key (256 bits of entropy).

Key properties:

  • One key per agent
  • Displayed only once at registration time
  • Cannot be retrieved or displayed again after registration
  • Stored as a hash in the encrypted agent registry, alongside the repository

Best practices:

  • Copy the key directly into the agent's environment file at registration time
  • Do not store keys in version control, wikis, or chat logs
  • If a key is compromised, remove the agent and re-register it

docs.title: Rotating an API Key
docs.text:
For a dashboard-managed agent, register it again from Agents → + Add Agent with the same name and its token: the server issues a new key, sends it to the agent and keeps the jobs. From the CLI, hitstor serve agent re-register AGENT_NAME --token TOKEN issues the new key (put it in the agent's agent.env).

For a CLI-based agent:

  1. Remove the agent, keeping its jobs: hitstor serve agent remove AGENT_NAME --keep-jobs
  2. Register it again: hitstor serve agent add AGENT_NAME
  3. Update the agent's configuration with the new key
  4. Restart the agent service

Snapshots are never deleted by removing an agent.

docs.title: Agent Registry
docs.text:
The agent registry is an encrypted data structure stored alongside the repository. It contains:

  • Agent names and hashed API keys
  • Agent metadata (registration time, last backup time, suspension, installed plugins)
  • Backup jobs, with their selection, schedule or backup plan, and latest results
  • For managed agents: encrypted token and agent address

The registry is encrypted with the repository key and cannot be read without the repository password.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Agent Deployment — install and configure agents on remote machines
  • Dashboard — view and manage agents from the web interface
  • Monitoring — set up alerts for stale agents

docs.title: Backup Jobs
docs.text: The dashboard Backups page (/backups) is the central place to define what gets backed up and when. Each backup job backs up one source of one machine and has a job_type that determines how data is collected. + New Backup Job opens the wizard described in Dashboard → Backups.

docs.title: Job Types
docs.text:
Type Collector Runs on files Agent filesystem scan via built-in plugin (hitstor-scanner-builtin, shipped with agent) or a custom scanner plugin (fs_scanner_plugin) Remote agent workload An installed workload plugin, for example SQL Server Remote agent (on the application host)

SaaS, built-in database, and cloud-VM job types were removed before the first public release (v0.1.0) — see the Roadmap. Legacy jobs of those types are loaded, but their schedules are disabled on startup.

docs.title: Filesystem Jobs
docs.text:
The default job type. The server assigns paths and schedule to an agent; the agent scans, chunks, and uploads new data.

  • Choose the folders in the wizard's selection tree; on the job page, Edit selection changes them
  • Enable Consistent snapshot to read from a volume snapshot (VSS on Windows, LVM or btrfs on Linux)
  • Set Full re-scan every N days to guard against silent corruption (0 disables it)
  • Backup Now asks whether to force a full re-scan or run an incremental backup

docs.title: Workload Jobs and Backup Plans
docs.text:
A workload job backs up the objects checked in the selection tree (for SQL Server, an instance or some of its databases) with a backup plan: each backup kind the plugin offers has its own schedule, and differential and log backups build on the job's own fulls. The wizard proposes:

Kind Default schedule Full Sundays at 01:00, on Differential Monday to Saturday at 01:00, on Log Every 15 minutes, off

Each kind can be switched off (on demand only). The server hands the agent the kind that is due next; when a full and a differential fall at the same time, the full runs and covers the differential. On the job page, Edit plan changes the plan, each kind's row has its own Run now, and Backup Now asks which kind to run.

docs.title: Results per object
docs.text: Each run reports on every object of the selection. The job page shows, per backup kind, the objects that were left out or failed and why; a run that stored some objects and failed others is marked partial. For SQL Server the page also shows each database's backup chain, and offers Run full backup now when a differential or log backup needs a new full. See SQL Server.

docs.title: Scheduling
docs.text:
Schedules are cron expressions with an IANA time zone, built with the schedule picker (every day, days of the week or month, every N minutes or hours) or typed as a 5-field expression. Jobs created before the picker may still run every N hours after their last backup; saving a new schedule replaces that with a cron expression. See Scheduling.

The agent daemon polls GetSchedule every 5 minutes (default, --poll-interval). "Backup Now" also sends a WakeUp RPC to dashboard-managed agents for immediate pickup.

docs.title: Retention
docs.text: Jobs do not delete old snapshots. Apply a retention policy with hitstor forget --keep-* (add --prune to reclaim the space); for workload snapshots the policy keeps whole backup chains. See Retention.

docs.title: Cancel Running Backups
docs.text: POST /api/backups/{id}/cancel aborts an active session. Sessions with no activity for 10+ minutes show a stalled badge on the dashboard.

docs.title: API
docs.text: See Dashboard HTTP API — Backup Jobs.

docs.title: Web Dashboard
docs.text: HitStor includes a built-in web dashboard for monitoring backup infrastructure, managing agents and backup jobs, restoring data, and configuring the server. The dashboard is served by the same hitstor serve process that handles gRPC connections.

docs.title: Accessing the Dashboard
docs.text:
The dashboard is available at:

https://SERVER_IP:8421

Replace SERVER_IP with the hostname or IP address of the HitStor server. The default dashboard port is 8421, configurable with --dashboard-port.

Once the server has a repository, the dashboard uses HTTPS with the same certificate as the gRPC port (see TLS Certificates); with the default self-signed certificate the browser shows a warning until you trust it. Plain-HTTP requests to the same port are redirected to HTTPS, so http://<server>:8421 also works. Before any repository exists, the server is in setup mode and serves the dashboard over plain HTTP.

docs.title: Signing In
docs.text:
Everyone signs in with a personal account: user name, password and a code from an authenticator app. Roles decide which pages, agents and actions each person gets. See Users and Access.

On a new server, or after upgrading from a version with a single dashboard password, the dashboard first asks to create the administrator, confirming the shared dashboard password. That password comes from the serve_dashboard_password configuration key; if none is configured, hitstor serve generates one at startup, stores its hash in the config file and prints the plaintext once in the server log (look for no dashboard password configured). Once the first administrator exists, the shared password no longer signs in.

Session cookies are HttpOnly and SameSite=Lax, and changes are refused when the browser reports a request from another site.

docs.title: Update Notifications
docs.text:
When update_check: true is set in the configuration (or Check for updates automatically is enabled under Settings → General), the server checks for new releases via the GitHub Releases API (or update_url) at startup and every 24 hours. Checks are off unless enabled. If a newer version is available, a notification banner appears at the top of every dashboard page:

HitStor v1.1.0 is available (current: v1.0.0). View release

The banner links to the release page on GitHub. You can also check manually from the CLI with hitstor version --check.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
The dashboard uses a fixed header bar, a sidebar with icon navigation, and a main content area. The header shows the repository name, the version and, on the right, the user menu: My account, the language and Sign out.

The sidebar groups pages by what you do with them, and shows only what your role allows:

  • Protection — Overview, Backups, Restores, Disaster Recovery
  • Infrastructure — Agents, Storage
  • Administration — Users and access, Audit log, Reports, Logs, Settings

Buttons for actions your role does not allow (for example removing an agent, or running a job on an agent you do not operate) are not shown.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The main page displays a summary of the backup infrastructure:

  • Number of agents and snapshots, backups running, last backup time, and storage usage
  • Agent health breakdown (OK, stale, never backed up)
  • Active Ransomware Sentinel alerts, with Resolve & Unsuspend
  • Quick links to the Agents and Storage pages

docs.title: Backups
docs.text:
Lists the backup jobs with their agent, last run, restore verification, and status. + New Backup Job opens a three-step wizard modeled on the backup jobs of enterprise backup tools:

  1. Selection. A tree shows every registered machine with its status and operating system. Expanding a machine lists its sources: the File system and each installed plugin (for example Microsoft SQL Server, then its instances and databases). Check what to back up; checking a container (a folder, an instance) backs up everything in it, including what is added later. A job backs up one source of one machine: once something is checked, the other sources lock until the selection is cleared. The side panel lists the selection and the source's options: exclude patterns and consistent snapshots for a file system, the plugin's options for a plugin.
  2. Target and schedule. The repository and when to run. A file system gets one schedule, nightly at 02:00 by default. A plugin source gets a backup plan with one schedule per backup kind: weekly fulls and daily differentials on, log backups every 15 minutes off (see Backup Jobs).
  3. Review. A summary of the job, with the schedule in words and its next run, and a suggested name.

A scheduled job shows Overdue when its latest backup is older than its schedule allows: the longest gap between two runs of its schedule plus half of it (for a weekly job, about 10½ days). Reports use the same rule.

Machines that are offline or suspended appear in the tree but cannot be expanded. On a job's page, Edit selection opens the same tree for that job's machine and source, with the current selection checked; the source options can change there too. Edit schedule (files) or Edit plan (plugins) changes when it runs. To back up another source, create another job.

docs.title: Restores
docs.text: Restores files from the snapshots of a protected agent, to the same or another agent, and restores plugin backups (for example a SQL Server database to a point in time) with Restore from a Plugin Backup. Active restores show their progress. See Restore.

docs.title: Disaster Recovery
docs.text: Guided full-system recovery of a protected agent onto a rebuilt host, and, under Bare metal, recovery media and single-use recovery tokens for Linux hosts. See Disaster Recovery and Bare-metal restore.

docs.title: Agents
docs.text:
Lists all registered agents with their current status, type (managed or CLI), number of jobs, and last backup time. Click an agent name to view its detail page.

Adding an agent from the dashboard (administrators):

  1. Click + Add Agent, then use Network Scan to scan a local subnet, or Manual Entry to connect to an agent by IP address
  2. In Register Agent, enter the agent name and the token (hitstor-agent show-id on the agent machine)
  3. Click Register Agent

The server connects to the agent over AgentService (port 8422), verifies the token, and sends API key + server address. See Agent Management and Agent Discovery.

docs.title: Agent Detail
docs.text:
Shows detailed information for a single agent:

  • Status, type, address, last backup, number of jobs and healthy jobs
  • Suspend Agent / Unsuspend Agent, + New Backup Job, Remove and Re-register, as your role allows
  • Live Status (managed agents) — host name, OS, version and other information queried from the agent
  • Plugins (managed agents) — installed workload plugins, installing a plugin package and configuring plugin credentials
  • Backup Jobs — the agent's jobs with their schedule, repository, last run and status

What a job backs up (folders, databases) is chosen in the job's selection tree, not on the agent page.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
The Storage page provides full repository management:

  • Repository list — view all configured repositories (local and S3) with status badges, disk usage bars, snapshot counts, and pack/index statistics
  • Create repository — initialize a new local or S3-compatible repository directly from the dashboard. Local repositories show available disk space and detect existing repos at the given path
  • Connect existing repository — if a repository already exists at a path (for example, after reinstalling), the dashboard detects it and connects instead of reinitializing
  • Disconnect repository — remove a repository from the configuration (does not delete data on disk)
  • Integrity check — run hitstor check on a repository with real-time progress via Server-Sent Events. Results show pass/fail status and any errors found
  • Prune — free space by removing unreferenced data, with confirmation dialog and live progress. Shows packs deleted, bytes freed, and indexes rewritten
  • Growth chart — visualize storage growth over time with configurable date range (30 days, 90 days, 6 months, 1 year, all) and granularity (daily, weekly)
  • Snapshots — each repository's page lists its snapshots; a snapshot's page browses its contents and restores individual files or whole paths. See Restore. (/snapshots redirects here.)

docs.title: Users and access, Audit log
docs.text: Accounts, roles, sessions and the tamper-evident audit log (administrators). See Users and Access.

docs.title: Reports
docs.text: Scheduled PDF reports and on-demand downloads (administrators). See Reports.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text: Server and agent log entries, filterable and exportable. Retention of the in-memory log and the optional rotating log file is set under Settings → General.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: Central hub for server configuration (administrators): general performance, TLS, network ports, Integrations (Gemini), notifications, email, and plugin packages. See Server Settings.

docs.title: My account
docs.text: Each user's profile, password, two-step verification, recovery codes, language, and open sessions. See Users and Access.

docs.title: Schedule Management
docs.text:
Schedules belong to backup jobs, not to agents. Users with the backup operator role (or administrators) set them:

  • In the New Backup Job wizard (step 2)
  • On a job's page, with Edit schedule (filesystem jobs) or Edit plan (workload jobs)

Agents running in daemon mode (hitstor-agent daemon) poll the server for schedule updates and execute backups accordingly. See Scheduling.

docs.title: JSON API
docs.text: The dashboard exposes a JSON API for programmatic access. All endpoints return JSON responses. The table below lists the agent and storage endpoints; see the Dashboard HTTP API reference for jobs, restores, settings and the rest.

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text:
Method Path Description GET /api/agents List all registered agents with status POST /api/agents Add a dashboard-managed agent (name, agent address, token) DELETE /api/agents/{name} Remove an agent (?keep_jobs=true keeps its jobs) POST /api/agents/{name}/suspend Suspend an agent POST /api/agents/{name}/unsuspend Resume a suspended agent POST /api/agents/{name}/schedule Legacy per-agent interval schedule (jobs carry their own schedules) POST /api/agents/{name}/repo Legacy per-agent target repository (jobs carry their own repository) POST /api/agents/{name}/browse Browse agent filesystem (managed agents) POST /api/agents/{name}/configure Configure agent backup paths (managed agents) GET /api/agents/{name}/info Query agent info (managed agents) GET /api/snapshots List all snapshots (supports ?agent=NAME filter) GET /api/stats Repository statistics (storage, deduplication, counts) GET /api/repos List all configured repositories POST /api/repos Create a new repository (local or S3) DELETE /api/repos/{name} Disconnect a repository POST /api/repos/test-s3 Test S3 endpoint connectivity POST /api/repos/detect Detect existing repository at a path GET /api/repos/{name}/growth Storage growth data for charting GET /api/repos/{name}/sessions Active backup sessions for a repository POST /api/repos/{name}/check Start integrity check (returns operation ID) POST /api/repos/{name}/prune Start prune operation (returns operation ID) GET /api/operations/{id}/events SSE stream for operation progress GET /api/disk-space Available disk space at a given path

The API uses the same session as the browser, so a request needs the session cookie (hitstor_session) of a user who completed two-step verification, and it can do only what that user's role allows. Without a session the API answers 401. In the examples below, SESSION is that cookie's value, and -k accepts the default self-signed certificate.

docs.title: Example: Add an Agent
docs.text:
curl -k -X POST https://localhost:8421/api/agents \
  -b "hitstor_session=SESSION" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"web-01","agent_addr":"192.168.1.50:8422","token":"a3f8c1d9e4b7..."}'

docs.title: Example: Browse Agent Filesystem
docs.text:
curl -k -X POST https://localhost:8421/api/agents/web-01/browse \
  -b "hitstor_session=SESSION" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"path":"/home"}'

docs.title: Example: List Agents
docs.text: curl -sk -b "hitstor_session=SESSION" https://localhost:8421/api/agents | jq .

docs.title: Prometheus Metrics
docs.text:
The dashboard exposes a Prometheus-compatible metrics endpoint once the server has a repository:

https://SERVER_IP:8421/metrics

This endpoint is unauthenticated (accessible without signing in) to allow Prometheus to scrape metrics without credential management. If this is a concern, restrict access at the network level.

See Monitoring for the full list of metrics and Prometheus configuration.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Agent Management — register and manage agents
  • Backup Jobs — filesystem and workload jobs, backup plans
  • Monitoring — configure Prometheus scraping and alerting
  • Scheduling — detailed scheduling configuration options
  • Security — dashboard authentication and hardening

docs.title: Monitoring and Alerting
docs.text: HitStor provides Prometheus metrics and webhook alerting to integrate with existing monitoring infrastructure.

docs.title: Prometheus Metrics
docs.text:
The server exposes a Prometheus-compatible metrics endpoint at:

https://SERVER_IP:8421/metrics

This endpoint is unauthenticated, allowing Prometheus to scrape without credential configuration. Restrict access at the network level if needed. It exists once the server has a repository; repository metrics describe the server's first repository.

docs.title: Repository and Agent Gauges
docs.text: Metric Type Description hitstor_snapshots_total gauge Total snapshots in the repository hitstor_packs_total gauge Total pack files in the repository hitstor_indexes_total gauge Total index files in the repository hitstor_repository_size_bytes gauge Total repository size in bytes hitstor_active_sessions gauge Current active backup sessions hitstor_registered_agents gauge Total registered agents hitstor_agents_ok gauge Agents with a backup within alert_stale_threshold (default 25 hours) hitstor_agents_stale gauge Agents whose last backup is older than alert_stale_threshold hitstor_agents_never gauge Agents that have never backed up

docs.title: Counters
docs.text:
Counters reset when the server restarts.

Metric Type Description hitstor_backups_completed_total counter Successful backups hitstor_backups_failed_total counter Failed or aborted backup sessions hitstor_bytes_received_total counter Bytes received from agents hitstor_chunks_received_total counter Chunks received from agents hitstor_checks_total counter Integrity checks run from the dashboard hitstor_check_errors_total counter Errors found by those checks hitstor_prunes_total counter Prune operations run from the dashboard hitstor_prune_freed_bytes_total counter Bytes freed by those prunes

docs.title: Per-Agent Metrics
docs.text: Metric Type Labels Description hitstor_agent_last_backup_timestamp_seconds gauge agent Unix timestamp of the agent's last successful backup (0 if never) hitstor_agent_schedule_enabled gauge agent Legacy per-agent schedule flag (1/0); backup jobs keep their own schedules hitstor_agent_schedule_interval_hours gauge agent Legacy per-agent interval in hours

docs.title: Prometheus Scrape Configuration
docs.text:
Add the following to your prometheus.yml:

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: "hitstor"
    scrape_interval: 30s
    scheme: https
    tls_config:
      ca_file: /etc/prometheus/hitstor-server.crt  # the server's certificate or CA
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["backup.example.com:8421"]

For multiple HitStor servers:

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: "hitstor"
    scrape_interval: 30s
    scheme: https
    tls_config:
      ca_file: /etc/prometheus/hitstor-ca.crt
    static_configs:
      - targets:
          - "backup-01.example.com:8421"
          - "backup-02.example.com:8421"

docs.title: Grafana Dashboard
docs.text:
To build a Grafana dashboard for HitStor:

  1. Add your Prometheus instance as a data source in Grafana.
  2. Create a new dashboard with panels for key metrics:

Suggested panels:

Panel Query Visualization Healthy Agents hitstor_agents_ok Stat Stale Agents hitstor_agents_stale Stat (red threshold > 0) Total Snapshots hitstor_snapshots_total Stat Storage Used hitstor_repository_size_bytes Stat (unit: bytes) Running Backups hitstor_active_sessions Stat Backup Rate rate(hitstor_backups_completed_total[1h]) Time series Failed Backups rate(hitstor_backups_failed_total[1h]) Time series (alert threshold) Data Ingestion rate(hitstor_bytes_received_total[5m]) Time series (unit: bytes/s) Last Backup per Agent hitstor_agent_last_backup_timestamp_seconds Table
  1. Set up Grafana alerts on hitstor_agents_stale > 0 and rate(hitstor_backups_failed_total[1h]) > 0.

docs.title: Webhook Alerting
docs.text: HitStor can send webhook notifications when backup sessions fail, agents go stale, or Sentinel detects a threat. Each event is a JSON POST with Content-Type: application/json.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Set the webhook URL in the config file:

# /etc/hitstor/config.yaml
alert_webhook_url: "https://hooks.example.com/hitstor"
alert_stale_threshold: 25
Key Type Default Description alert_webhook_url string (none) URL to POST alert payloads to alert_stale_threshold integer 25 Hours without a backup before an agent is considered stale alert_notifier_plugins list (none) Notifier plugins to load

These keys can also be set under Settings → Notifications, which can send a test event. They are read at startup: restart the server after changing them.

docs.title: Alert Events
docs.text: Every event has the same fields: event, server (always hitstor), timestamp, agent, hostname (when known), message, and details.

docs.title: backup_failed
docs.text:
Sent immediately when a backup fails: the agent reports that the job failed (for example, a database that cannot be read), the agent disconnects during the upload, or the snapshot cannot be finalized. For failures reported by the agent, details carries job, job_id and kind, and hostname is empty.

{
  "event": "backup_failed",
  "server": "hitstor",
  "timestamp": "2026-02-21T03:05:00Z",
  "agent": "web-server-01",
  "hostname": "web-server-01",
  "message": "backup failed: agent disconnected during upload",
  "details": {"session_id": "3f9a...", "chunks_received": 1520}
}

docs.title: agent_stale
docs.text:
Sent when an agent has not completed a backup within the stale threshold. The server checks every 5 minutes; agents that have never backed up are not reported.

{
  "event": "agent_stale",
  "server": "hitstor",
  "timestamp": "2026-02-21T14:00:00Z",
  "agent": "staging-app",
  "message": "no backup in 2d1h (threshold: 1d1h)",
  "details": {"last_backup": "2026-02-19T12:30:00Z", "threshold_hours": 25}
}

docs.title: threat_detected
docs.text: Sent by Ransomware Sentinel when it reports a threat at or above its confidence threshold.

docs.title: Cooldown and Recovery
docs.text:
To avoid alert fatigue, HitStor applies cooldown logic:

  • After sending a stale alert for an agent, it does not re-alert until the threshold duration has elapsed again.
  • When a stale agent completes a successful backup, the alert state is cleared. If the agent goes stale again, a new alert is sent.
  • Failed backup alerts have no cooldown -- each failure triggers a notification.

docs.title: Notifier Plugins
docs.text:
For custom notification delivery (Slack, PagerDuty, email, etc.), use notifier plugins instead of or in addition to the webhook.

Configure notifier plugins in the config file:

# /etc/hitstor/config.yaml
plugin_dir: /usr/lib/hitstor/plugins
alert_notifier_plugins:
  - slack
  - pagerduty

Each name maps to a binary hitstor-notifier-<name>, looked up in plugin_dir and then in PATH. Notifier plugins receive the same events as the webhook (over the plugin gRPC interface) and can transform them for their target system. See the Plugins documentation for details on writing and installing plugins.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Dashboard -- view metrics and agent status in the web UI
  • Scheduling -- configure backup schedules to keep agents active
  • Troubleshooting -- diagnose stale agents and failed backups

docs.title: Reports
docs.text: HitStor emails PDF reports on a schedule, and any of them can be downloaded at any time. Administrators manage them under Administration → Reports. Sending needs email set up; downloading does not.

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
Report Covers For Protection summary The last 7 or 30 days Managers: are the servers protected? Daily backup status The last 24 hours The team that runs the backups: what ran, what failed and why

Both start with a verdict, Everything is protected, Protected, with warnings or Action needed, and the reason in one sentence, followed by the figures and a list of what needs attention.

The protection summary shows the success rate, how many jobs are up to date, the data backed up, the storage used, a chart of the runs per day (successful, partial, failed), what needs attention, each agent and job, and each repository's use and free space.

The daily status shows the runs of the last 24 hours, the failures with their reason (the same failure repeated, such as hourly log backups failing all night, is one row with its count and time span), how each job stands, and every run with its duration and size.

docs.title: When a job is up to date
docs.text:
Each backup kind of a job (the files of a file job; the full, differential and log backups of a database plan) has an objective taken from its schedule: the longest wait between two scheduled runs, and half again. A kind backed up every day must have a good backup from the last 36 hours; an hourly log backup, from the last 90 minutes. One missed run already shows; a slow run does not.

Status Meaning Protected The latest good backup is within the objective Warning Within the objective, but the latest run failed, left objects out, or its test restore failed Late The latest good backup is older than the objective Never backed up Scheduled, but no good backup yet On demand Not scheduled, so no objective

A report also flags active ransomware alerts and repository disks with less than 10 % free.

docs.title: Run history
docs.text: Jobs remember only their latest outcome, so the server keeps a history of every run (successful, partial or failed) for reports: one file per month next to the agent registry, encrypted with the repository key, kept for 13 months. Successful runs from before the history existed are read from the snapshots; failures are known only from when it started, and reports say so.

docs.title: Scheduled reports
docs.text:
New scheduled report asks for:

  • Type and, for the protection summary, the period it covers (last 7 or 30 days).
  • Recipients: one address per line, up to 50. Each scheduled report has its own, so the daily status can go to the backup team and the weekly summary to management.
  • When to send it: the same schedule picker as backup jobs, with its time zone.
  • Agents: some, or none ticked to cover every agent, including later ones.
  • Language of the report and its email.

The email says the verdict in its subject and body, and carries the PDF. Send now sends it at once; View opens the PDF as it would be sent now. If the server was down when a report was due, it is sent on start if less than six hours late; older slots are skipped, and the list shows why a report was not sent.

Reports are kept in the server's config.yaml under reports: (see the configuration reference).

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text: HitStor is a backup and restore product for Windows and Linux: filesystems in the core, and applications through installable workload plugins. The roadmap exists to make it excellent at that. Work that does not improve backing up and restoring data fast, safely, and verifiably is out of scope by default.

docs.title: Shipped
docs.text: Item Notes Deduplication & encryption engine FastCDC chunking, Zstd, AES-256-GCM, scrypt KDF Server / agent architecture gRPC over TLS, thick agent chunks and compresses locally Web dashboard Jobs, agents, storage, restores, progress via SSE Users, roles and two-step verification Personal accounts with roles scoped to agents, mandatory TOTP, hash-chained audit log Email Invitations and password-reset links over SMTP or Microsoft 365 (OAuth 2.0) Scheduled PDF reports Protection summary and daily backup status, emailed on a schedule or downloaded Incremental backups & synthetic full Parent-snapshot reuse, periodic full rescan Advanced scheduling 5-field cron with L, D#N and DL, schedule builder, timezone-aware with DST handling Agent auto-discovery Network scan for unregistered agents Snapshot restore File-tree browse, granular and whole-path restore Restore verification Automated post-backup restore checks per job Consistent snapshots VSS (Windows), LVM and btrfs (Linux) Guided disaster recovery Multi-job full-system restore onto a rebuilt host Bare-metal restore (Linux) ReaR rescue media built per host, extended attributes and system profile captured with --bare-metal Benchmarks Reproducible backup/restore harness, optional restic comparison Ransomware Sentinel Gemini telemetry over filesystem snapshots (optional) Workload plugins Signed .hpk packages installed per agent, locally or from the dashboard; backup and point-in-time restore through the agent; chain-aware retention Backup plans Workload jobs schedule full, differential, and log backups of one selection separately; results per database SQL Server mssql plugin over VDI: full, differential, and log backups; point-in-time restore

docs.title: Now
docs.text: Item Goal Windows bare-metal restore WinPE recovery media, NTFS security descriptors, and BCD rebuild — see below

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Item Goal Remote filesystem restore Restore to an agent in another network or a cloud VM Restore performance Parallel restore streams and resume after interruption

docs.title: Bare-metal restore
docs.text:
Bare-metal restore rebuilds a Linux host from a blank disk. Relax-and-Recover (ReaR) builds bootable rescue media on each host, recreates the disk layout, and reinstalls the bootloader; HitStor restores the files. Backups taken with --bare-metal also capture extended attributes (SELinux contexts, file capabilities, POSIX ACLs) and the system profile (partition table, filesystem UUIDs, LVM, /etc/fstab).

Windows is the remaining part. It needs:

  1. Boot media — a WinPE image carrying the agent.
  2. Richer file metadata — Windows security descriptors, which the current snapshot format does not capture.
  3. Bootloader reconstruction — BCD on Windows.

Restoring files alone onto a blank disk produces an unbootable system, so these land together rather than as independent features.

docs.title: Permanently removed
docs.text:
These were removed from the product before the first public release (v0.1.0) and are not planned to return in their original form:

  • Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace backup
  • The built-in database integrations (PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle)
  • Cloud VM agentless backup (GCP, AWS, Azure) and VMware/vSphere
  • The workload collector plugin type that served them

Database backup now comes back as installable workload plugins that run on the database host, starting with SQL Server.

Existing config.yaml files containing collector_plugins or the related integration keys still load; those keys are simply ignored (unknown fields).

docs.title: Also not on the roadmap
docs.text: Autonomous DR (auto-failover, LLM-generated bootstrap scripts, DNS promotion, scheduled RPO/RTO drills) remains out of scope. If demand returns, it should build on agent-based restore rather than bespoke cloud provisioning.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Disaster Recovery
  • Restore
  • Sentinel
  • Codebase Overview

docs.title: Backup Scheduling
docs.text: HitStor supports several approaches to scheduling automatic backups. Choose the method that best fits your infrastructure.

docs.title: Server-Managed Scheduling
docs.text: The recommended approach is server-managed scheduling, where backup schedules are configured centrally and agents poll the server for their next run time.

docs.title: Configure from the Dashboard
docs.text:
1. Open the Dashboard at https://SERVER_IP:8421.
  2. Navigate to Backups and click + New Backup Job. Step 2 of the wizard sets the schedule with the schedule picker (see Schedule Picker); a plugin source gets a backup plan, one schedule per backup kind.
  3. To change the schedule of an existing job, open it and expand Edit schedule (or Edit plan for a workload job). It uses the same picker; Edit as cron expression switches to the raw expression.
  4. The dashboard validates the expression and shows it in words with its next runs.
  5. Click Save Schedule (or Save plan).

The server stores each job's schedule with the job, in the agent registry. Agents running in daemon mode pick up changes automatically.

docs.title: Interval Mode (legacy)
docs.text:
Jobs created before cron schedules (or through the API with schedule_hours) run every N hours:

  • How it works: next_run = last_backup + interval_hours; after a failed run, the next try is 15 minutes later
  • Timezone: Not applicable (relative to last backup time)

The dashboard no longer creates interval jobs. Saving a new schedule on such a job replaces the interval with a cron expression; the picker starts from the nearest equivalent.

docs.title: Schedule Picker
docs.text:
Backup jobs, of files or of a plugin, set their schedule with a picker modeled on the schedule sets of enterprise backup tools, and store the result as a cron expression:

Option Settings On demand only The job runs only with Backup Now Repeating → Every day Start time Repeating → Days of week Weekdays, and optionally weeks of the month (1st to 5th, Last); start time Repeating → Days of month Days 1 to 31 and Last day; start time. Days a month does not have are skipped Repeating → Every… Every 5 to 30 minutes, or every 1 to 12 hours at a given minute; optionally only between two hours and only Monday to Friday

Each schedule takes a time zone (the browser's by default for a new job; Server local uses the server's). The picker shows the schedule in words and its next runs, and Edit as cron expression switches to the raw expression. A new filesystem job starts from every day at 2:00 AM. In a backup plan each kind starts from its usual schedule: fulls on Sundays at 1:00 AM, differentials Monday to Saturday at 1:00 AM (both on), and log backups every 15 minutes (off until you switch them on). In a plan, a kind is either repeating or off (on demand only).

docs.title: Cron Expression Mode
docs.text:
Standard 5-field cron syntax for precise, timezone-aware scheduling:

┌───────────── minute (0-59)
│ ┌───────────── hour (0-23)
│ │ ┌───────────── day of month (1-31)
│ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1-12)
│ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of week (0-6, Sun=0)
│ │ │ │ │
* * * * *

Supported syntax:

Syntax Example Meaning Wildcard * Every value Specific value 5 Only at 5 List 1,15 At 1 and 15 Range 1-5 1 through 5 Step */15 Every 15 units Range with step 0-30/10 0, 10, 20, 30 Last day of month L (day of month) The last day of each month Nth weekday 0#1 (day of week) The first Sunday of the month (#1 to #5) Last weekday 5L (day of week) The last Friday of the month

Names (MON, JAN), 7 for Sunday, and macros such as @daily are not accepted. When both day of month and day of week are restricted, a day matching either runs, as in standard cron (0 2 1 * 1 runs on the 1st and on every Monday).

Common examples:

Expression Description 0 2 * * * Daily at 2:00 AM 0 3 * * 1-5 Weekdays at 3:00 AM 30 1 * * 0 Sundays at 1:30 AM 0 */6 * * * Every 6 hours 0 22 1 * * 1st of each month at 10:00 PM */15 * * * * Every 15 minutes 0 23 L * * Last day of each month at 11:00 PM 0 2 * * 0#1 First Sunday of each month at 2:00 AM

Timezone handling:

  • Select a timezone from the dropdown (IANA format, e.g. America/New_York).
  • If no timezone is selected (Server local), the server's local timezone is used. An unknown timezone falls back to UTC.
  • Cron expressions are evaluated in the selected timezone, handling DST transitions automatically:
    • Spring forward: If a scheduled time falls in the skipped hour, that day's run is skipped; the next run is the next matching day.
    • Fall back: If a scheduled time falls in the repeated hour, the backup runs on the first occurrence.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. The agent calls the GetSchedule RPC on the server.
  2. The server evaluates the schedule (cron expression, backup plan or interval) and responds with the next run time (next_run). For a backup plan it also says which backup kind is due.
  3. The agent sleeps until next_run, then executes the backup.
  4. After the backup completes, the agent calls GetSchedule again for the next run.

This approach allows administrators to change schedules from the dashboard without restarting or reconfiguring agents.

docs.title: Missed Window Recovery
docs.text:
If the server or agent is offline when a backup was due:

  • On the next poll, the server detects that now > next_run and signals the agent to run immediately.
  • After the catch-up backup, the schedule advances to the next future occurrence (no double-runs).
  • This works for interval, cron and backup-plan schedules.

A failed run is not retried on every poll: a cron or plan schedule waits for its next slot, and an interval job retries after 15 minutes.

docs.title: Agent Daemon Mode
docs.text:
Daemon mode is the client-side component of server-managed scheduling. Start the agent in daemon mode:

hitstor-agent daemon

In daemon mode, the agent:

  • Runs as a long-lived process
  • Polls the server for its backup schedule via the GetSchedule RPC (default: every 5 minutes; --poll-interval, minimum 1 minute)
  • Executes backups when now >= next_run_unix for any enabled job
  • Reports backup results back to the server
  • Handles transient connection failures with automatic retry

docs.title: Systemd Service (Linux)
docs.text:
Enable the daemon as a systemd service:

sudo systemctl enable hitstor-agent
sudo systemctl start hitstor-agent

The service unit runs hitstor-agent daemon --config /etc/hitstor/agent-config.yaml with restart-on-failure.

docs.title: Windows Service
docs.text:
Register the daemon as a Windows Service:

hitstor-agent service install
hitstor-agent service start

The Windows installer already does this. The service starts automatically on boot. See Agent Deployment for full Windows setup instructions.

docs.title: Systemd Timer (Alternative)
docs.text:
If you prefer cron-style scheduling managed at the OS level rather than server-managed scheduling, use a systemd timer that runs a one-shot hitstor-agent backup.

Note

Versions before 0.2.1 installed a hitstor-agent.timer that only started the daemon again; current packages remove it. Use your own units, as below, for one-shot backups.

docs.title: Create the Units
docs.text:
The agent must already be able to reach the server: /etc/hitstor/agent.env holds HITSTOR_AGENT_SERVER and HITSTOR_AGENT_API_KEY once the agent is registered.

# /etc/systemd/system/hitstor-backup.service
[Unit]
Description=HitStor one-shot backup
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=oneshot
EnvironmentFile=/etc/hitstor/agent.env
ExecStart=/usr/bin/hitstor-agent backup /etc /home

# /etc/systemd/system/hitstor-backup.timer
[Unit]
Description=Run a HitStor backup daily at 2 AM

[Timer]
OnCalendar=*-*-* 02:00:00
Persistent=true

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target

docs.title: Enable the Timer
docs.text:
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now hitstor-backup.timer

docs.title: Customize the Schedule
docs.text:
Change OnCalendar in the timer, or override it:

sudo systemctl edit hitstor-backup.timer

[Timer]
OnCalendar=
OnCalendar=*-*-* 03:00:00

docs.title: OnCalendar Syntax
docs.text:
The OnCalendar directive uses systemd calendar event syntax. Common examples:

Expression Schedule *-*-* 02:00:00 Daily at 2:00 AM *-*-* 00/6:00:00 Every 6 hours (midnight, 6 AM, noon, 6 PM) *-*-* *:00:00 Every hour Mon *-*-* 03:00:00 Every Monday at 3:00 AM *-*-01 04:00:00 First day of each month at 4:00 AM *-*-* 02:00:00,14:00:00 Twice daily at 2:00 AM and 2:00 PM

Verify the schedule with systemd-analyze:

systemd-analyze calendar "*-*-* 02:00:00"

docs.title: Timer vs. Daemon Mode
docs.text:
Feature Daemon Mode Timer Mode Schedule source Server (dashboard) Local systemd timer Central management Yes No (per-machine) Dynamic schedule changes Yes (via dashboard) Requires systemd edit Process lifecycle Long-running Starts per backup Workload (plugin) jobs and dashboard restores Yes No Server connection Persistent On-demand

Daemon mode is recommended for most deployments because it enables centralized schedule management.

docs.title: Windows Task Scheduler
docs.text:
On Windows systems where the agent is not registered as a Windows Service, use Task Scheduler as an alternative:

  1. Open Task Scheduler (taskschd.msc).
  2. Create a new basic task.
  3. Set the trigger to the desired schedule (for example, daily at 2:00 AM).
  4. Set the action to start a program:
    • Program: hitstor-agent.exe in the agent's installation folder
    • Arguments: backup C:\Users C:\Data
  5. Save the task.

The command line does not read agent.env (only the daemon and the service do), so give the task the server and key: add --server HOST:8420 --api-key KEY to the arguments, or set agent_server and agent_api_key in a config file passed with --config.

For server-managed scheduling on Windows, use daemon mode via the Windows Service instead.

docs.title: Scheduling Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use cron expressions for production deployments. They provide precise, timezone-aware scheduling that handles DST transitions and server restarts correctly.
  • Stagger backup times across agents to avoid overloading the server with simultaneous backups. With cron expressions, use different minutes (e.g., 0 2 * * * for one agent, 15 2 * * * for another).
  • Use off-peak hours (for example, 01:00 to 05:00) to minimize impact on production workloads.
  • Always set a timezone when using cron expressions to avoid ambiguity across servers in different locations.
  • Set the stale threshold (alert_stale_threshold) to slightly more than the backup interval. For daily backups, 25 hours is a reasonable default.
  • Monitor scheduling via the dashboard and Prometheus metrics to ensure backups run on time.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Agent Deployment -- install agents and configure systemd units
  • Monitoring -- set up alerts for missed backups
  • Dashboard -- manage schedules from the web interface

docs.title: Security
docs.text: This page documents the HitStor security model, covering encryption, key management, authentication, and system hardening.

docs.title: Data Encryption
docs.text:
All data stored in the repository is encrypted with AES-256-GCM (Galois/Counter Mode). Encryption is applied before data is written to storage — by hitstor for local backups, and by the server for agent backups (agents chunk and compress locally and send the chunks over TLS) — ensuring that the repository contents are unreadable without the password.

Each blob (chunk of data) is encrypted with a unique nonce. The authenticated encryption provided by GCM ensures both confidentiality and integrity -- any tampering with encrypted data is detected on read.

docs.title: Key Derivation
docs.text:
Each repository has a random 64-byte master key: an EncKey (AES-256-GCM encryption of blobs) and an IDKey (HMAC-SHA256 blob identification). The master key is stored in the repository's keys/ directory, encrypted with a key derived from the repository password using scrypt with the following parameters and a random 64-byte salt:

Parameter Value Purpose N 32768 CPU/memory cost factor r 8 Block size p 1 Parallelization factor

These parameters are designed to make brute-force attacks computationally expensive. Because the data keys are random rather than derived from the password, guessing the password is the only way to reach them.

docs.title: Blob Identification
docs.text:
Blob IDs are computed as HMAC-SHA256 using the repository's IDKey. This prevents content-guessing attacks: an attacker who knows the plaintext content of a file cannot determine whether it exists in the repository without knowing the password.

BlobID = HMAC-SHA256(IDKey, plaintext)

Without the IDKey, an attacker cannot correlate known plaintext with stored blobs.

docs.title: TLS
docs.text:
All gRPC communication between agents and the server is encrypted with TLS. The server either auto-generates a self-signed certificate or uses custom certificates provided by the administrator.

Configuration Encryption Certificate Verification Auto-generated (default) Yes Agent pins the server certificate on first connection, or trusts it via agent_ca_cert Custom certificate Yes Standard CA verification or agent_ca_cert Let's Encrypt Yes Standard CA verification (no extra config)

TLS is always enabled. There is no option to disable transport encryption.

See TLS Certificates for detailed configuration.

docs.title: Agent Authentication
docs.text:
HitStor uses two authentication mechanisms for agents:

Agent tokens (dashboard-managed agents):

  • 64-character hexadecimal string (256 bits of entropy)
  • Generated automatically on the agent's first start
  • Stored at /etc/hitstor/agent-token on the agent (mode 0600; C:\ProgramData\HitStor\agent-token on Windows, readable only by SYSTEM and Administrators)
  • Stored encrypted (AES-256-GCM) on the server in the agent registry
  • Used by the server to authenticate gRPC calls to the agent (registration, browsing, plugin installation, restores)
  • Retrievable any time with hitstor-agent show-id
  • Verified using constant-time comparison to prevent timing attacks

API keys (all agents):

  • 64-character hexadecimal string (256 bits of entropy)
  • One key per agent
  • Generated using a cryptographically secure random number generator
  • For dashboard-managed agents: sent to the agent automatically during registration
  • For CLI-registered agents: displayed once at registration time and cannot be retrieved again
  • Stored as a hash in the encrypted agent registry

An agent must present a valid API key with every backup gRPC request. The server verifies the key against the hashed value in the registry.

docs.title: Repository Password
docs.text:
The repository password is the root secret for all encryption operations. It is:

  • Provided at runtime through a password file (password_file per repository), the HITSTOR_PASSWORD environment variable, or --password/--password-file. Repositories created from the dashboard store it in a password file next to the config file (<name>.password, mode 0600): protect that directory
  • Used, through scrypt, to unlock the master key (EncKey and IDKey)
  • Required to read or write any data in the repository

If the password is lost, the repository data is irrecoverable.

docs.title: Dashboard Authentication
docs.text:
The dashboard uses personal accounts with roles scoped to agents and mandatory two-step verification (TOTP). Passwords are stored as argon2id hashes; sessions time out after inactivity, sensitive changes ask to sign in again, accounts lock after repeated failures, and a hash-chained audit log records sign-ins, changes and denied requests. See Users and Access.

Session cookies have the following security properties:

Property Value Purpose HttpOnly true Prevents JavaScript access to the cookie SameSite Lax Not sent on cross-site subrequests; changes from other sites are also refused by origin checks Secure over HTTPS Not sent over plain HTTP

The /metrics endpoint is excluded from authentication to allow Prometheus scraping. Restrict access to this endpoint at the network level if needed.

docs.title: Systemd Hardening
docs.text:
The HitStor server systemd unit includes security hardening directives that restrict the server process:

[Service]
User=hitstor
Group=hitstor

# Filesystem protection
ProtectSystem=strict
ReadWritePaths=/var/lib/hitstor /var/log/hitstor /etc/hitstor
ProtectHome=true
PrivateTmp=true

# Privilege restrictions
NoNewPrivileges=true

# Kernel protection
ProtectKernelTunables=true
ProtectKernelModules=true
ProtectControlGroups=true

These directives:

  • Run the server as the unprivileged hitstor user
  • Prevent the server from writing outside /var/lib/hitstor, /var/log/hitstor and /etc/hitstor
  • Block privilege escalation
  • Isolate the process from home directories, kernel tunables, kernel modules and control groups

If the service fails with status=226/NAMESPACE (some Hyper-V VMs, containers, WSL), the unit file says which lines to comment out.

docs.title: Verifying Hardening
docs.text:
Check the security score of the unit:

systemd-analyze security hitstor-server

Lower scores mean a more restricted service. Review any items marked as "UNSAFE" and assess whether you can restrict them further with a drop-in (systemctl edit hitstor-server).

docs.title: Security Checklist
docs.text:
Use this checklist when deploying HitStor in production:

  • [ ] Use a strong repository password (at least 16 characters, randomly generated)
  • [ ] Store the password in a file with 0600 permissions, not on the command line
  • [ ] Use custom TLS certificates from a trusted CA (the dashboard uses the same certificate)
  • [ ] Create personal accounts with the least role each person needs, and remove the ones no longer used
  • [ ] Restrict dashboard port (8421) to management networks
  • [ ] Restrict the /metrics endpoint to Prometheus scraper IPs
  • [ ] Enable systemd hardening (included by default in packaged units)
  • [ ] Ensure agent token files (/etc/hitstor/agent-token) have 0600 permissions
  • [ ] Restrict agent gRPC port (8422) to the server's IP address
  • [ ] Rotate API keys if compromise is suspected (re-register the agent; see Agent Management)
  • [ ] Run hitstor check --read-data periodically to verify repository integrity
  • [ ] Keep HitStor updated to receive security fixes

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• TLS Certificates -- configure production TLS
  • Agent Management -- API key registration and rotation
  • Troubleshooting -- diagnose security-related issues

docs.title: Ransomware Sentinel
docs.text: HitStor Sentinel (internal/sentinel) monitors backup session telemetry for ransomware-like behavior using Google Gemini. When risk is elevated, it can alert administrators and apply protective actions such as agent suspension and storage retention locks.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
After every backup session finalizes, the server:

  1. Gathers up to 10 prior snapshots for the same host as a baseline.
  2. Sends the current session's telemetry plus that baseline to Gemini for analysis.
  3. If the analysis reports a threat with confidence at or above HITSTOR_SENTINEL_THRESHOLD (default 0.8), the server:
  4. Suspends the agent's credentials, blocking further backups from that host.
  5. Locks the configured storage bucket with an immutable retention hold, so ransomware cannot delete historical snapshots even with valid credentials.
  6. Fires an alert, visible via GET /api/alerts and any configured webhook/notifier.

This only runs the containment steps above the confidence threshold — most backups complete with Sentinel silently finding nothing.

docs.title: Telemetry Signals
docs.text:
• New versus unchanged files (mass modification)
  • Bytes added versus bytes processed (encrypted data stops deduplicating)
  • New files with extensions typical of ransomware
  • Session duration, compared to the host's own history

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Sentinel is enabled by default when the server starts. It is configured entirely through environment variables read at hitstor serve startup — there is no hitstor config set equivalent. The Gemini API key/model fall back to the encrypted integrations.* values in config.yaml (set via Settings → Integrations) when the Sentinel-specific variables are unset.

See Environment Variables → Sentinel for the full variable list, defaults, and the three supported retention-lock backends (GCS, S3, Azure Blob).

Configure alerting alongside existing webhook and notifier plugins:

alert_webhook_url: https://hooks.slack.com/services/...
alert_notifier_plugins:
  - slack
plugin_dir: /usr/local/lib/hitstor/plugins

docs.title: Dashboard Alerts
docs.text: Active Sentinel alerts appear at the top of the dashboard's Overview page, with the agent, host, confidence and reason. Resolve & Unsuspend (administrators) closes the alert and unsuspends the agent so it can back up again. Through the API, list alerts with GET /api/alerts, close one with POST /api/alerts/{id}/resolve, and unsuspend the agent separately with POST /api/agents/{name}/unsuspend.

docs.title: Retention Lock
docs.text: For supported object storage backends (GCS, S3, Azure Blob), Sentinel can trigger immutable retention locks on the backup bucket to prevent ransomware from deleting historical snapshots — even with valid, unrevoked credentials. This is separate from the repository's own backend (local/S3); the lock targets whichever bucket HITSTOR_SENTINEL_BACKEND_TYPE and its bucket variable point at.

docs.text:
