docs.title: Estados en el dashboard
docs.text: Las etiquetas de estado (badges) se escriben en masculino singular, porque se comparten entre tareas, sesiones, restauraciones y agentes: completado, fallido, omitido, pendiente, en ejecución, desactivado, atrasado, inactivo, suspendido, nunca. Los valores técnicos cortos se mantienen: ok, info, cli.

docs.title: Reglas
docs.text:
• No traducir: bloques de código, comandos, flags, nombres de archivos, rutas, claves de configuración (serve_dashboard_password), variables de entorno, nombres de API ni salidas de la CLI (la CLI se mantiene en inglés).
  • Los nombres de elementos de la interfaz (botones, páginas) van en el idioma del dashboard al que se refiere el texto: en español, los nombres en español.
  • En la documentación (MkDocs), los encabezados traducidos conservan el anchor en inglés: ## Instalar { #install }. En los README de GitHub no se usa esa sintaxis: los enlaces internos apuntan al anchor del encabezado en español.

docs.title: Workload Plugin Architecture
docs.text: Status: implemented (phases 1–4): plugin framework and remote installation, workload backup and restore, backup-chain retention, the SQL Server plugin, and the dashboard pages driven by plugin-declared fields. The first plugin built on this architecture is Microsoft SQL Server backup through the Virtual Device Interface (VDI). It supersedes the "workload collector plugin type" entry under Permanently removed in the roadmap.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• The core stays workload-agnostic. A HitStor agent without plugins backs up files exactly as today. The core never parses SQL Server (or any other application) data.
  • Plugins are optional, separately versioned software. A plugin is installed only on the agents that need it, can be upgraded or removed without reinstalling the agent, and ships as its own release asset.
  • Installing a plugin adds capabilities to that agent only. The server and dashboard offer a workload's jobs and restores only for agents that report the plugin.
  • Adding a new workload needs no core or dashboard changes. Forms, the object picker, and restore planning come from the plugin.

Non-goals for the first version: agentless backup, plugins running on the server, and third-party plugin marketplaces.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
┌──────────────── HitStor server ────────────────┐
            │  Plugin package store                           │
            │  Per-agent inventory: installed plugins and     │
            │  their capabilities                             │
            │  Jobs and restores, rendered from each          │
            │  plugin's declared schema                       │
            └───────▲──────────────────────────┬──────────────┘
      inventory     │                          │ InstallPlugin (package push)
      (heartbeat)   │                          │ jobs, restores
                    │                          ▼
┌───────────────────┴──────────── Agent ──────────────────────────────┐
│  Core pipeline: chunk · dedup · compress · encrypt · upload           │
│  Plugin manager: install, verify signature, version, remove           │
│     <data dir>/plugins/<id>/<version>/                                │
│                          │ gRPC over go-plugin, one process per job   │
│               ┌──────────▼───────────┐                                │
│               │  hitstor-plugin-<id> │──► application (e.g. SQL VDI)  │
│               └──────────────────────┘                                │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

A plugin never talks to the server. It reads from and writes to the local application; the agent owns everything that touches the repository.

docs.title: Plugin package
docs.text:
A plugin is distributed as a package file: hitstor-plugin-<id>-<version>-<os>-<arch>.hpk. It is a zip archive with:

Entry Purpose plugin.yaml Manifest (below) bin/hitstor-plugin-<id>[.exe] Plugin executable LICENSE, README.md Optional documentation SIGNATURE Detached ed25519 signature over the canonical package digest

docs.title: Manifest
docs.text:
id: mssql                      # unique, lowercase, [a-z0-9-]
name: Microsoft SQL Server
version: 1.0.0                 # semver; independent from the agent version
type: workload
protocol_version: 1            # workload protocol version
min_agent_version: 0.2.0
platforms: [windows/amd64]
entrypoint: bin/hitstor-plugin-mssql.exe
publisher: hitstor             # selects the trusted key

This is the manifest inside a package. The plugins/<id>/plugin.yaml kept with the source omits platforms and entrypoint: hitstor-pluginkit pack fills them in for each target, so one source manifest yields one package per platform.

The capabilities (backup kinds, restore options, and form fields) are not duplicated in the manifest. The agent asks the plugin for them through GetMetadata, so the binary is the single source of truth.

docs.title: Signing and trust
docs.text:
Plugins run with the agent's privileges (LocalSystem on Windows, root on Linux) and usually hold administrative credentials for the application, so the agent verifies every package before installing it:

  1. The signature must validate against a trusted publisher key. The HitStor release key is embedded in the agent; operators can add their own keys (plugin_trusted_keys) for in-house plugins.
  2. platforms must include the agent's OS and architecture.
  3. min_agent_version and protocol_version must be supported.

Unsigned packages are rejected unless the agent explicitly enables plugin_allow_unsigned (meant for plugin development only).

docs.title: Agent plugin manager
docs.text:
• Layout: <data dir>/plugins/<id>/<version>/ holds the unpacked package. On Windows the data directory is C:\ProgramData\HitStor. Only administrators and the agent service account may write there.
  • Registry: <data dir>/plugins/installed-plugins.json records each plugin's id, active version, status (active, degraded, unregistered), and the metadata last returned by GetMetadata.
  • Install and upgrade: the package is unpacked into a new version directory and verified, then the plugin is launched once for a GetMetadata handshake. Only then does the active version switch. A failed upgrade leaves the previous version active. Old versions are removed after a successful switch, never while a job is using them.
  • Remove: refused while a job is running. Snapshots made by the plugin stay in the repository and remain restorable as plain files.
  • Inventory: the agent reports installed plugins and their metadata to the server with its schedule poll, so the server always knows what each agent can do.
  • Runtime: the plugin starts as a subprocess for each job and exits afterwards. A crash fails that job only; the agent keeps running.

docs.title: Installation channels
docs.text: Channel How Local hitstor-agent plugin install <file.hpk>, plus list, info, upgrade, and remove; browse, configure, test-backup, and test-restore help diagnose a plugin on the agent without the server Remote Upload the package to the server once, then install it on chosen agents from the dashboard. The server streams the package over a new AgentService.InstallPlugin RPC, and the agent applies the same checks as a local install.

docs.title: Workload protocol
docs.text:
New service Workload in api/proto/hitstor/plugin/v1/workload.proto, served over the existing go-plugin handshake:

RPC Purpose GetMetadata Plugin id, version, protocol version, capabilities, and the form fields for jobs, restores, and settings Configure Connection settings (instance, authentication) Browse Tree of selectable objects, e.g. instance → databases, for the dashboard object picker Backup Takes the selection and backup kind; streams back one or more items: name, bytes, and an opaque metadata blob PlanRestore Takes the metadata of candidate items and a target point; returns the ordered list of items to apply (e.g. full → differential → logs) Restore Receives the planned items' bytes in order and applies them, with the restore options from the form

docs.title: Items in snapshots
docs.text:
Each item a plugin produces is stored as a virtual file in the snapshot, under /<plugin id>/<object path>/<item name>. For example:

/mssql/<instance>/<database>/full-20260101T020000.000Z.bak
/mssql/<instance>/<database>/full-20260101T020000.000Z.bak.meta.json
/mssql/<instance>/<database>/log-20260101T021500.000Z.trn

The agent feeds each item's stream through the same chunk, dedup, compress, and encrypt pipeline as regular files. As a result, deduplication, encryption, retention, verification, and replication work without changes. The metadata blob, which the core never interprets, is stored next to the item. The snapshot is tagged with plugin:<id>, kind:<kind>, copy-only for a copy-only full, and one obj:<object> per object it holds.

Each run also reports per-object outcomes: an object the plugin left out (for example a database that does not support the requested kind) or one that failed, with the reason. The server keeps them with the job, per backup kind, and a run that stored some objects and failed others counts as partial.

Because items are ordinary files, they can also be restored to a folder through the normal file restore. This is the fallback when the plugin is unavailable.

docs.title: Restore flow
docs.text:
1. The operator picks an agent, an object, and a target point in the dashboard. The restore form comes from the plugin schema.
  2. The server collects the candidate items' metadata from the plugin's snapshots and sends it to the agent.
  3. The agent asks the plugin to PlanRestore and returns the plan to the server.
  4. The server streams the planned items to the agent, which pipes them into the plugin's Restore in order.

The core only ships bytes in the order the plugin asked for. All application-specific logic stays in the plugin, such as backup chains, LSNs, and recovery options.

docs.title: Retention
docs.text: A retention policy must not delete an item that a still-retained item depends on (for example, a full backup that later differentials or logs need). Using the plugin:, kind:, and obj: tags, when a policy keeps a differential or log backup of an object, forget also keeps the earlier backups of that object, on the same host and plugin, back to its base: the previous full that is not copy-only (tagged copy-only). A kept differential needs only that full; a kept log also needs the logs in between. A kept full, copy-only or not, restores on its own. The rule needs no plugin-specific knowledge and errs on the side of keeping more.

docs.title: Server and dashboard
docs.text:
• Workload jobs (job_type: workload) store the plugin id, the selected objects, the plugin settings, and the backup options as opaque values; only the plugin interprets them.
  • A workload job carries a backup plan: each backup kind of the same selection has its own schedule (for SQL Server, for example, weekly fulls, daily differentials, and log backups every 15 minutes), or runs on demand only. The server picks the kind that is due next and hands it to the agent as the run's backup kind, so agents need no notion of plans. When a full and a differential fall due at the same time, the full runs and fills both slots.
  • The dashboard renders job, restore, and settings forms from the fields each plugin declares in GetMetadata (FieldSpec: key; scope settings, object, backup, or restore; type string, bool, number, choice, or password; labels and help per language, default, choices). password fields are accepted only in scope object: they stay on the agent, encrypted, and are never sent back to the dashboard. Plugins never ship HTML.
  • The agent page lists the plugins installed on that agent, with install, upgrade, and remove actions. Settings → Plugins manages uploaded packages. Removing a plugin that a job still uses is refused.

docs.title: First plugin: SQL Server (VDI)
docs.text: Aspect Decision Package hitstor-plugin-mssql-<version>-windows-amd64.hpk Location plugins/mssql/ in this repository, released as its own asset Data path VDI (sqlvdi.dll, IClientVirtualDeviceSet2) through COM in pure Go, with no cgo, plus T-SQL through go-mssqldb Backup kinds Full (optionally COPY_ONLY), differential, transaction log Restore Full chain with NORECOVERY/RECOVERY, point in time (STOPAT), restore under a new name with MOVE Authentication Per instance, set from the object tree and kept on the agent, encrypted: the agent service account, a Windows account, or a SQL login (all need sysadmin). Never in jobs or config.yaml Metadata LSNs (first, last, checkpoint, database_backup_lsn), backup times, and recovery model, read from msdb.dbo.backupset

docs.title: Delivery phases
docs.text:
1. Plugin framework: package format, signing, agent plugin manager, local CLI, and inventory reporting.
  2. Workload protocol: items as virtual files in the agent pipeline, and generic plugin jobs on the server.
  3. SQL Server plugin: VDI backup and restore of every kind, plus point in time.
  4. Dashboard and docs: remote install, object picker, schema-driven forms, and the roadmap update.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Plugin Development Guide: existing plugin types (storage, notifier, hook, scanner)
  • Codebase Overview
  • Roadmap

docs.title: Release Process
docs.text: Releases are built and published by GitHub Actions when a version tag is pushed.

docs.title: Cut a Release
docs.text:
git tag -a v1.2.0 -m "HitStor 1.2.0"
git push origin v1.2.0

The tag starts two workflows:

Workflow What it does .github/workflows/release.yml Runs go test ./..., then make release-assets VERSION=1.2.0, then builds the signed workload plugin packages (make plugin-packages), checks each one with hitstor-pluginkit verify, regenerates SHA256SUMS, and creates the GitHub release v1.2.0 with every file in dist/ attached. Release notes are generated from the commits since the previous tag. .github/workflows/docker-publish.yml Builds the Docker image for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64 and pushes it to GHCR (ghcr.io/hooperits/hitstor) tagged 1.2.0, 1.2, and latest. It can also be started by hand (workflow_dispatch).

The version embedded in the binaries and in the artifact names is the tag without the leading v. Plugin packages keep their own version, taken from each plugins/<id>/plugin.yaml.

docs.title: Plugin Signing Key
docs.text:
The release job runs in the GitHub environment release, which accepts deployments only from v* tags. Its secret HITSTOR_PLUGIN_SIGNING_KEY holds the base64 ed25519 seed of the official plugin key, and only the Build signed plugin packages step receives it. Each package is then verified against the official public keys embedded in the agent (hitstor-pluginkit verify), so a missing or wrong secret fails the release instead of publishing packages that agents would reject.

To rotate the key, generate a new pair with hitstor-pluginkit keygen, add the new public key to OfficialKeys in internal/pluginpkg/trust.go (keep the old one so existing packages stay valid), release an agent with it, and only then replace the secret.

After the workflows finish, deploy the documentation if it changed:

make docs-deploy

docs.title: Release Assets
docs.text:
make release-assets runs clean, build-all, pkg-linux, pkg-windows, the .run installers for amd64 and arm64, and checksums. For VERSION=1.2.0, dist/ contains:

dist/
├── hitstor-server-1.2.0-linux-amd64.run
├── hitstor-server-1.2.0-linux-arm64.run
├── hitstor-agent-1.2.0-linux-amd64.run
├── hitstor-agent-1.2.0-linux-arm64.run
├── hitstor_1.2.0_amd64.deb
├── hitstor-1.2.0-1.x86_64.rpm
├── hitstor-agent_1.2.0_amd64.deb
├── hitstor-agent-1.2.0-1.x86_64.rpm
├── hitstor-1.2.0-windows-amd64-setup.exe
├── hitstor-agent-1.2.0-windows-amd64-setup.exe
└── SHA256SUMS

The release workflow then adds the plugin packages to dist/ (for example hitstor-plugin-mssql-0.5.0-windows-amd64.hpk and the example plugin for Linux and Windows) and regenerates SHA256SUMS.

scripts/install-agent.sh downloads hitstor-agent-VERSION-linux-ARCH.run from the latest release, so both .run architectures must be present.

docs.title: Build Locally
docs.text:
To reproduce the release assets on a workstation (requires Go, nfpm, NSIS and Python with Pillow for the Windows icon):

make release-assets VERSION=1.2.0
make plugin-packages PLUGIN_KEY_FILE=mykey.key   # or PLUGIN_UNSIGNED=1
make checksums

make release VERSION=1.2.0 builds the same assets plus the Docker image tarball (dist/hitstor-1.2.0-docker.tar.gz, requires Docker).

docs.title: VERSION Variable
docs.text:
The VERSION variable is passed to all build steps via Go linker flags (-ldflags). It controls:

  • The version string embedded in the binary (hitstor version)
  • Package version in .deb, .rpm and Windows installer metadata
  • Docker image tag (hitstor:VERSION)
  • Output file names in dist/

Two additional variables are set automatically:

Variable Source Example VERSION Makefile argument (default: dev) 1.2.0 COMMIT git rev-parse --short HEAD 9341885 DATE date -u +%Y-%m-%d 2026-02-24

docs.title: Partial Builds
docs.text: Command What It Builds make release-linux .deb + .rpm packages only make installers .run installers (amd64) only make pkg-windows Windows .exe installers only make release-docker Docker image tarball only make checksums SHA256SUMS for everything in dist/

docs.title: Clean
docs.text:
Remove all build artifacts:

make clean

This deletes bin/, dist/, and site/.

docs.title: Server Preparation
docs.text:
This page covers what to do on a fresh Ubuntu server before installing HitStor. It covers OS-level prerequisites only. For post-installation steps (init, serve, systemd), see Server Setup.

Using the .run installer?

The Linux Quick Install (.run) handles user creation, directory setup, configuration, and service startup automatically via an interactive wizard; the repository is then created from the dashboard. You only need the System Updates, Firewall, and Storage sections from this page.

docs.title: System Updates
docs.text:
Start with a fully updated system:

sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y

docs.title: Required Packages
docs.text:
Ubuntu ships with systemd by default. Install the additional packages HitStor depends on:

sudo apt install -y ca-certificates openssl
Package Purpose systemd Service management (pre-installed on Ubuntu) ca-certificates TLS certificate validation for agent connections openssl TLS certificate generation

Note

The .deb post-install script automatically creates the hitstor system user, group, and all required directories. No manual user creation is needed.

docs.title: Firewall Configuration
docs.text:
HitStor uses two TCP ports:

Port Protocol Service 8420 TCP gRPC — agent communication 8421 TCP Web dashboard and Prometheus metrics

docs.title: Install and Configure ufw
docs.text: sudo apt install ufw

docs.title: Open Both Ports
docs.text:
Warning

Always allow SSH (port 22) before running ufw enable, or you may lose remote access to the server.

sudo ufw allow 22/tcp comment "SSH"
sudo ufw allow 8420/tcp comment "HitStor gRPC"
sudo ufw allow 8421/tcp comment "HitStor Dashboard"
sudo ufw enable

Verify the rules:

sudo ufw status verbose

docs.title: Restrict Dashboard to LAN
docs.text:
If the dashboard should only be accessible from the local network:

sudo ufw allow from 10.0.0.0/24 to any port 8421 proto tcp comment "HitStor Dashboard (LAN)"

Replace 10.0.0.0/24 with your actual network range.

docs.title: Storage Considerations
docs.text:
Repository data lives at /var/lib/hitstor/repo by default.

  • Estimate storage: raw data size divided by expected deduplication ratio. Typical dedup ratios range from 2x to 10x depending on how similar the backed-up data is across snapshots.
  • Dedicated volume: mount a separate partition or volume at /var/lib/hitstor to isolate backup storage from the OS disk.
  • Filesystem: ext4 or XFS. Both work well; XFS performs slightly better with large files.
  • Permissions: the post-install script sets /var/lib/hitstor to mode 750, owned by hitstor:hitstor.
# Example: mount a dedicated volume
sudo mkfs.xfs /dev/sdb1
sudo mkdir -p /var/lib/hitstor
echo '/dev/sdb1 /var/lib/hitstor xfs defaults 0 2' | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab
sudo mount /var/lib/hitstor

docs.title: TLS Certificates
docs.text: When no certificate is configured, HitStor generates a self-signed certificate on startup and saves it in the repository directory (server.crt, server.key) so it survives restarts; before the server has a repository, the certificate is kept in memory only. This is fine for testing, but production deployments should use proper certificates.

docs.title: Self-Signed with OpenSSL
docs.text:
sudo mkdir -p /etc/hitstor/tls
sudo openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:4096 -nodes \
    -keyout /etc/hitstor/tls/server.key \
    -out /etc/hitstor/tls/server.crt \
    -days 365 -subj "/CN=HOSTNAME"
sudo chmod 600 /etc/hitstor/tls/server.key
sudo chown hitstor:hitstor /etc/hitstor/tls/server.key /etc/hitstor/tls/server.crt

Replace HOSTNAME with the server's FQDN or IP address.

docs.title: Let's Encrypt
docs.text:
sudo apt install -y certbot
sudo certbot certonly --standalone -d backup.example.com

For detailed TLS configuration, see TLS Certificates.

docs.title: .run Installer
docs.text:
The .run installer with the interactive wizard handles everything:

  1. Creates system group and user hitstor, and lets it read the systemd journal
  2. Creates directories: the data directory (default /var/lib/hitstor), /var/log/hitstor, /etc/hitstor
  3. Installs the binary and systemd service
  4. Writes configuration files from wizard answers (mode 600)
  5. Enables and starts the service
  6. Verifies the service is running and ports are listening

It does not create a repository: open the dashboard to create or connect one.

docs.title: .deb Package
docs.text:
When you install the .deb package with dpkg -i, the post-install script handles:

  1. Creates system group hitstor (if it does not exist)
  2. Creates system user hitstor with home /var/lib/hitstor and shell /usr/sbin/nologin
  3. Adds the hitstor user to the systemd-journal group (for the dashboard Logs page)
  4. Creates directories: /var/lib/hitstor, /var/log/hitstor, /etc/hitstor, /usr/lib/hitstor/plugins
  5. Sets ownership of /var/lib/hitstor and /var/log/hitstor to hitstor:hitstor and mode 750
  6. Copies server.env.example to server.env and config.yaml.example to config.yaml (mode 600) if they do not exist
  7. Runs systemctl daemon-reload to pick up the new service file

After installing the package, review the configuration files and create a repository, from the dashboard or with hitstor init (see Server Setup).

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
