Forgetting a snapshot removes only the snapshot metadata. The actual data packs remain on disk until prune is run. Use --prune to automatically run prune after forgetting.

An exclusive lock is acquired on the repository for the duration of the operation.

docs.title: Flags
docs.text:
Flag Type Default Description --keep-last int 0 Keep the N most recent snapshots --keep-hourly int 0 Keep N hourly snapshots --keep-daily int 0 Keep N daily snapshots --keep-weekly int 0 Keep N weekly snapshots --keep-monthly int 0 Keep N monthly snapshots --keep-yearly int 0 Keep N yearly snapshots --keep-tag string Keep snapshots with this tag (repeatable) --host string Only apply policy to snapshots from this host --path string Only apply policy to snapshots with this path --dry-run bool false Only show what would be removed --prune bool false Run prune after forgetting to reclaim space

Plus all global flags, including --repo-name for multi-repo setups.

docs.title: Retention Semantics
docs.text:
Retention flags use union semantics: a snapshot is kept if it matches any of the active --keep-* rules. For example, with --keep-last 3 --keep-daily 7, a snapshot is kept if it is among the 3 most recent or among the 7 most recent daily snapshots.

The --host and --path flags filter which snapshots the policy applies to. Snapshots not matching the filter are left untouched.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Forget a specific snapshot:

hitstor forget --repo /backups/hitstor --password "secret" a1b2c3d4

Apply a retention policy:

hitstor forget --repo /backups/hitstor --password "secret" \
  --keep-last 5 --keep-daily 7 --keep-weekly 4 --keep-monthly 12

Preview what would be removed:

hitstor forget --repo /backups/hitstor --password "secret" \
  --keep-last 3 --dry-run

Forget and prune in one step:

hitstor forget --repo /backups/hitstor --password "secret" \
  --keep-last 5 --prune

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• After forgetting snapshots without --prune, HitStor prints a reminder to run hitstor prune.
  • --keep-tag keeps any snapshot that has the specified tag, regardless of other retention rules.
  • The policy applies to all in-scope snapshots as one set, not per host or path. For workload snapshots (for example SQL Server), it also applies to each database's own backups, and a kept differential or log backup keeps the backups it needs to restore. See Workload Backup Chains.

docs.title: hitstor init
docs.text: Initialize a new backup repository.

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text: hitstor init [flags]

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Creates a new encrypted backup repository at the location specified by --repo. This sets up the directory structure (data/, index/, snapshots/, keys/, locks/, config) and generates a master key encrypted with the provided password using scrypt key derivation.

The repository must not already exist. The repository ID is printed on success.

docs.title: Flags
docs.text: This command uses only the global flags.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Initialize a local repository:

hitstor init --repo /backups/hitstor --password "my-secret-password"

Initialize an S3 repository:

hitstor init \
  --repo s3:http://localhost:9000/hitstor-backups \
  --password "my-secret-password" \
  --s3-access-key minioadmin \
  --s3-secret-key minioadmin

Using environment variables:

export HITSTOR_REPO=/backups/hitstor
export HITSTOR_PASSWORD="my-secret-password"
hitstor init

docs.title: hitstor jobs
docs.text:
Manage scheduled backup jobs (multi-repo aware).

Note: Full job management (editing, workload jobs with backup plans, running and cancelling) is done in the dashboard. The CLI covers listing, creating file jobs, and repairing orphaned jobs.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: hitstor jobs [command]

docs.title: Subcommands
docs.text: Command Description list List configured backup jobs (--agent <name> filters by agent; --orphans shows only orphaned jobs) create Create a file backup job in the agent registry of the repository given by --repo-name orphans List jobs whose agent is no longer registered reattach Re-attach jobs to an agent: --agent <name> (required) with --all-orphans or --job-id <id> (repeatable)

docs.title: Flags for create
docs.text:
• --name (required)
  • --repo-name (required)
  • --job-type (only files is supported; workload jobs are created in the dashboard)
  • --path (repeatable)
  • --interval-hours, --cron, --timezone, --agent-name

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
hitstor --config /etc/hitstor/config.yaml jobs list

hitstor --config /etc/hitstor/config.yaml jobs create \
  --name "Daily /home" \
  --repo-name Production \
  --job-type files \
  --path /home \
  --interval-hours 24

create stores the job in the agent registry of the --repo-name repository, which is also where the job's backups go. A running server reads jobs from the registry of its first repository (by name), so create jobs that back up to another repository from the dashboard. For production job management use the dashboard Backups page.

docs.title: hitstor prune
docs.text: Remove unreferenced data from the repository.

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text: hitstor prune [flags]

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Removes pack files, index entries, and blobs that are no longer referenced by any snapshot. Run this after forget to reclaim storage space.

Prune performs a mark-and-sweep garbage collection:

  1. Scans all snapshots to determine which blobs are still referenced.
  2. Identifies pack files containing only unreferenced blobs (deleted entirely) or a mix of referenced and unreferenced blobs (repacked).
  3. Writes new pack files containing only the referenced blobs from mixed packs.
  4. Deletes obsolete pack files and updates indexes.

An exclusive lock is acquired on the repository for the duration of the operation.

docs.title: Flags
docs.text:
Flag Type Default Description --dry-run bool false Only show what would be removed --max-repack-size string Limit total bytes repacked (e.g., 500MiB, 2GiB)

Plus all global flags, including --repo-name for multi-repo setups.

docs.title: Size Suffixes
docs.text:
Suffix Meaning B Bytes KiB, MiB, GiB, TiB Binary units (1024-based) KB, MB, GB, TB Decimal units (1000-based)

If no suffix is given, the value is treated as bytes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Prune unreferenced data:

hitstor prune --repo /backups/hitstor --password "secret"

Preview what would be removed:

hitstor prune --repo /backups/hitstor --password "secret" --dry-run

Limit repacking to 500 MiB:

hitstor prune --repo /backups/hitstor --password "secret" --max-repack-size 500MiB

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Prune is also available as part of forget --prune, which combines both operations.
  • The operation reports the number of packs deleted, packs repacked, bytes freed, and indexes updated.

docs.title: hitstor repo
docs.text: Repository management commands (multi-repository aware).

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: hitstor repo [command]

docs.title: Subcommands
docs.text: Command Description list List configured repositories from the multi-repo config create <name> <path> Create and initialize a new repository: local (an absolute <path>), or S3 with --type s3 --endpoint <host> --bucket <bucket> --access-key ... --secret-key ... [--region ...]. The repository password comes from --password or the global password options and is saved in <name>.password next to the config file; S3 keys are stored encrypted delete <name> Remove a repository from the config (does not delete data) health Show operational health for the selected repository

docs.title: Global Flags (relevant)
docs.text:
• --repo-name <name> — Select a named repository from the repositories: list in config.
  • --config /etc/hitstor/config.yaml — Recommended when running on the server.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# List all repositories known to this server
hitstor --config /etc/hitstor/config.yaml repo list

# Create a new local repo (creates password file next to config)
hitstor --config /etc/hitstor/config.yaml repo create MyRepo /data/myrepo

# Health check on a named repo
hitstor --config /etc/hitstor/config.yaml --repo-name MyRepo repo health

See also: hitstor config show (shows modern repositories section when present).

docs.title: hitstor restore
docs.text: Restore files from a snapshot.

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text: hitstor restore [flags] <snapshot-id> <target-path>

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Restores all files from the specified snapshot to the target directory. The snapshot can be identified by its full 64-character hex ID, a unique short prefix, or the keyword latest (which resolves to the most recent snapshot by timestamp).

Both arguments are required: the snapshot ID and the target path where files will be written.

docs.title: Flags
docs.text:
Flag Type Default Description --include string Restore only this path, relative to the snapshot root (for example documents/important.pdf from a backup of /home/user/documents), and everything under it. Exact path, not a glob (repeatable)

Plus all global flags, including --repo-name for multi-repo setups.

docs.title: Snapshot ID Resolution
docs.text:
HitStor supports three ways to identify a snapshot:

  • Full ID — the complete 64-character hex string
  • Short prefix — a unique prefix of the snapshot ID (e.g., a1b2c3d4). If the prefix is ambiguous (matches multiple snapshots), an error is returned.
  • latest — resolves to the snapshot with the most recent timestamp

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Restore the latest snapshot:

hitstor restore --repo /backups/hitstor --password "secret" latest /tmp/restore

Restore a specific snapshot by short ID:

hitstor restore --repo /backups/hitstor --password "secret" a1b2c3d4 /tmp/restore

Restore only specific files:

hitstor restore --repo /backups/hitstor --password "secret" latest /tmp/restore \
  --include "documents/important.pdf"

docs.title: hitstor serve
docs.text: Start the gRPC backup server.

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
hitstor serve [flags]
hitstor serve agent add|list|remove|re-register|assign-repo ...
hitstor serve user add|list|grant|passwd|reset-2fa|disable|enable|remove ...

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Starts the HitStor gRPC server that accepts remote agent backups over TLS. The server handles deduplication, encryption, and storage on behalf of remote agents. It also starts the web dashboard on a separate HTTP port.

If no TLS certificate is provided, a self-signed certificate is generated automatically. The dashboard uses the same certificate: once a repository is configured it is served over HTTPS on the dashboard port, and a plain-HTTP listener on the next port (dashboard port + 1) redirects to it. With no repository configured the server starts in setup mode and serves only the dashboard, over plain HTTP.

Dashboard sign-in uses personal accounts with roles and two-step verification; see Users and Access. The serve_dashboard_password setting is only used until the first administrator exists.

docs.title: Flags
docs.text:
Flag Type Default Description --port int 8420 gRPC listen port --tls-cert string Path to TLS certificate file --tls-key string Path to TLS private key file --dashboard-port int 8421 Dashboard listen port --advertise-addr string auto-detected Address sent to agents during registration (host:port)

Plus all global flags.

docs.title: serve agent add <name>
docs.text: Register a new backup agent. Outputs a 64-character hex API key that the agent uses for authentication. Save this key immediately — it cannot be displayed again.

docs.title: serve agent list
docs.text: List all registered agents with their names, creation dates, and last backup times.

docs.title: serve agent remove <name>
docs.text: Remove a registered agent. The agent will no longer be able to connect. Its backup jobs are deleted too unless --keep-jobs is given.

docs.title: serve agent re-register <name> --token <token>
docs.text: Re-register an existing agent, keeping its jobs, with the token printed by hitstor-agent show-id. --addr sets the agent's address; --skip-rpc only updates the registry without contacting the agent.

docs.title: serve agent assign-repo <name> <repo-name>
docs.text:
Set the repository the agent's future jobs use.

hitstor agents is the same command group; see agents.

docs.title: serve user ...
docs.text:
Manage dashboard users from the server console, for example when no administrator can sign in:

Subcommand Description add <name> --grant <role>[=agent1,agent2] Create a user (repeat --grant; --display-name, --email). Prints a temporary password list List users grant <name> --grant ... Replace a user's roles passwd <name> Reset the password to a temporary one and end the user's sessions reset-2fa <name> Remove the user's authenticator and recovery codes; they set it up again at the next sign-in disable <name> / enable <name> Stop or allow sign-in; enable also lifts a lockout remove <name> Delete a user

Roles are admin, backup_operator, restore_operator, and viewer. See Users and Access.

The serve agent and serve user commands work on the repository where the server keeps its agent registry and users (the first configured repository by name), so --repo-name is not needed; naming another repository prints a warning, because the running server does not read it.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Start the server with default settings:

hitstor serve --repo /var/lib/hitstor/repo --password "secret"

Start with custom TLS certificates:

hitstor serve --repo /var/lib/hitstor/repo --password "secret" \
  --tls-cert /etc/hitstor/tls/server.crt \
  --tls-key /etc/hitstor/tls/server.key

Register a new agent:

hitstor serve agent add webserver-01 \
  --repo /var/lib/hitstor/repo --password "secret"

List registered agents:

hitstor serve agent list \
  --repo /var/lib/hitstor/repo --password "secret"

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The first repository (by name) must be on a local filesystem (not S3): the agent registry, dashboard users, and audit log are stored alongside it.
  • Graceful shutdown on SIGINT/SIGTERM.
  • The dashboard is served as an embedded HTML5 application with no external dependencies.

docs.title: hitstor snapshots
docs.text: List all snapshots in the repository.

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text: hitstor snapshots [flags]

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Lists all snapshots stored in the repository, sorted by time (newest first). By default, output is a formatted table showing each snapshot's short ID, timestamp, hostname, tags, file count, and total size.

Use --json for machine-readable JSON output.

Alias: hitstor ls

docs.title: Flags
docs.text:
Flag Type Default Description --host string Show only snapshots from this hostname --path string Show only snapshots that include this backed-up path

Plus all global flags, including --repo-name to target a specific repository in multi-repo setups.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
List all snapshots:

hitstor snapshots --repo /backups/hitstor --password "secret"

Filter by hostname:

hitstor snapshots --repo /backups/hitstor --password "secret" --host webserver-01

JSON output:

hitstor snapshots --repo /backups/hitstor --password "secret" --json

docs.title: JSON (--json)
docs.text:
[
  {
    "id": "a1b2c3d4",
    "time": "2025-01-15T10:30:00Z",
    "hostname": "myhost",
    "paths": ["/home/user/documents"],
    "total_files": 150,
    "total_size": 47185920
  }
]

docs.title: hitstor verify-restore
docs.text: Test-restore a snapshot and re-hash files (restore verification).

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text: hitstor verify-restore <snapshot-id> [flags]

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Restores a snapshot (or a sample of its files) to a temporary directory, re-chunks each restored file with the repository chunker, and compares content blob IDs to the snapshot tree.

This is the primary trust signal that a filesystem backup is actually restorable — it round-trips real data through restore and re-chunking rather than just checking metadata.

Use latest as the snapshot ID to verify the most recent snapshot. Tab completion for snapshot IDs is available.

docs.title: Flags
docs.text:
Flag Type Default Description --max-files int 0 (all) Limit the number of files verified --max-bytes uint64 0 (unlimited) Limit total bytes verified --keep-temp bool false Keep the temporary restore directory instead of cleaning it up

Plus all global flags, including --repo-name for multi-repo setups.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Verify the latest snapshot in full:

hitstor verify-restore latest --repo /backups/hitstor --password "secret"

Sample-verify a large snapshot, capping at 500 files:

hitstor verify-restore a1b2c3d4 --max-files 500

Verify and keep the temp restore for manual inspection:

hitstor verify-restore latest --keep-temp

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Every backup job's dashboard entry can also run this automatically after each backup — see Guided disaster recovery.
  • A non-zero exit code means either a mismatch was found or the verification itself errored; mismatches are printed to stderr with the mismatched path and reason.
  • With --json, output is a single JSON object (ok, snapshot_id, files_checked, files_sampled, bytes_checked, symlinks_ok, sampled, duration, mismatches, error, restore_target) instead of the human-readable summary.

docs.title: hitstor version
docs.text: Display version information and check for updates.

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text: hitstor version [--check] [--json]

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Prints the HitStor version, commit hash, build date, and platform.

With --check, contacts the GitHub Releases API to determine if a newer version is available.

docs.title: Flags
docs.text: Flag Description --check Check for available updates --json Output in JSON format

docs.title: Print version
docs.text:
hitstor version

Output:

hitstor v0.2.0 (commit a1b2c3d, built 2026-02-27, linux/amd64)

docs.title: Check for updates
docs.text:
hitstor version --check

Output when an update is available:

Update available: v0.3.0 (current: v0.2.0)
Release: https://github.com/hooperits/hitstor/releases/tag/v0.3.0

Output when up to date:

You are running the latest version (v0.2.0).

Output when the check fails (network error):

Could not check for updates.

docs.title: Automatic Version Check
docs.text:
When update_check: true is set in the server configuration (it is off unless set; Settings → General in the dashboard also turns it on), the server checks for updates every 24 hours. If a newer version is available, a notification banner appears at the top of the web dashboard.

See Configuration Reference for the update_check and update_url settings.

docs.title: User Guide
docs.text: The HitStor User Guide covers everything you need to know to protect your data with encrypted, deduplicated backups. Whether you are backing up a single laptop or managing retention policies across multiple servers, this guide walks you through every step.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text: Guide Description Getting Started End-to-end tutorial that takes you from initializing a repository to restoring files. Backup Create backups, exclude files, use tags, tune parallelism, and understand deduplication. Restore Restore full snapshots or individual files, resolve snapshot IDs, and verify restored data. Snapshots List, filter, compare, and inspect snapshots stored in your repository. Retention Define retention policies, remove old snapshots with forget, and reclaim space with prune. Configuration Manage the config file, environment variables, and interactive setup wizard. Plugins Discover, install, and configure storage backends, notifiers, hooks, scanner plugins, and workload plugins. SQL Server Back up and restore SQL Server databases through the mssql workload plugin, with backup plans of full, differential, and log backups. Disaster Recovery Rebuild a whole host from its file backups with the guided dashboard wizard. Bare-Metal Restore Recover a machine with a blank disk from bootable recovery media.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Before following the guides in this section, make sure you have HitStor installed. See the Installation Guide for platform-specific instructions.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
Throughout the User Guide the following conventions are used:

  • Commands prefixed with $ are run in a terminal.
  • Text in UPPER_CASE (such as SNAPSHOT_ID) represents a value you must replace with your own.
  • Optional flags are shown in square brackets: [--flag VALUE].
  • Long commands are split across multiple lines with \ for readability.

docs.title: Backup
docs.text: The hitstor backup command creates a new snapshot of one or more directories. Each snapshot captures the full state of the specified paths at the time the backup runs, but thanks to content-defined chunking and deduplication, only new or changed data is actually written to the repository.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
hitstor backup --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" /path/to/backup

This creates a snapshot containing every file under /path/to/backup.

docs.title: Backing Up Multiple Paths
docs.text:
You can specify more than one source path in a single backup:

hitstor backup --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" \
    /home/user/documents \
    /home/user/photos \
    /etc

All listed paths are included in the same snapshot.

docs.title: Command-Line Excludes
docs.text:
Use --exclude to skip files or directories that match a pattern:

hitstor backup --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" \
    --exclude "*.tmp" \
    --exclude "node_modules" \
    /home/user/projects

Patterns use Go's filepath.Match glob syntax (*, ?, [...]). Each pattern is matched against the file or directory name and against its path relative to the backup root; an excluded directory is skipped with everything under it:

Pattern Matches *.log All files ending in .log cache/ Any directory named cache (a trailing / matches directories only) build Any file or directory named build, at any depth data/temp The path data/temp relative to the backup root (no leading /)

** is not supported: * does not cross /, and a name pattern such as build already matches at any depth.

docs.title: Config File Excludes
docs.text:
You can also define excludes with the top-level exclude key of the configuration file (see Configuration):

exclude:
  - "*.tmp"
  - ".cache"
  - "node_modules"

docs.title: Merging Behavior
docs.text: Excludes from both sources are merged at runtime. A file is excluded if it matches any pattern from either the command line or the config file. Command-line patterns do not replace config-file patterns; they add to them.

docs.title: Tags
docs.text:
Tags let you label snapshots for easier filtering later. Use --tag (repeatable) to attach one or more tags:

hitstor backup --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" \
    --tag project-alpha \
    --tag weekly \
    /data/project-alpha

Tags appear in the hitstor snapshots output and can be used with --keep-tag in retention policies. See Retention for details.

docs.title: Host Override
docs.text:
By default HitStor records the system hostname in each snapshot. If you back up the same data from multiple machines, or if your hostname changes, you can override it:

hitstor backup --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" \
    --host webserver-01 \
    /var/www

The host value is used by forget when applying per-host retention policies.

docs.title: Dry Run Mode
docs.text:
To preview what a backup would do without writing any data, pass --dry-run:

hitstor backup --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" \
    --dry-run \
    /data

The command scans the source paths, reports file counts and estimated data sizes, but does not create a snapshot or write any packs.

docs.title: Parallel Workers
docs.text:
HitStor processes files concurrently. The --parallel flag controls the number of worker goroutines:

hitstor backup --repo /path/to/repo --password "secret" \
    --parallel 4 \
    /data

The default behavior auto-detects the number of CPUs and caps at 8 workers. On I/O-bound workloads (network storage, spinning disks) you may get better throughput with fewer workers; on fast SSDs you can try increasing the count.

Situation Recommended --parallel NVMe SSD, many small files 6--8 Spinning disk 1--2 Network mount (NFS, SMB) 2--4 S3 backend 4--8

docs.title: Progress Display
docs.text:
While the backup runs on a terminal, HitStor prints a live progress bar showing:

  • Percentage done
  • Files processed out of the total scanned
  • Throughput
  • Estimated time remaining

The bar updates in place. When the output is redirected to a file or pipe, HitStor prints one line per file instead (new or unchanged, with its size). Both end with a summary of new and unchanged files, data added, and duration.

docs.title: How Deduplication Works
docs.text: HitStor uses a three-layer deduplication strategy to minimize storage consumption:

docs.title: 1. Content-Defined Chunking (FastCDC)
docs.text: Files are split into variable-length chunks using the FastCDC algorithm. Unlike fixed-size splitting, FastCDC is resilient to insertions and deletions: if you add a paragraph to the beginning of a large file, only the first few chunks change while the rest remain identical.

docs.title: 2. Chunk-Level Deduplication
docs.text: Every chunk is identified by its cryptographic hash. Before writing a chunk to the repository, HitStor checks whether a chunk with the same hash already exists. If it does, the chunk is simply referenced rather than stored again.

docs.title: 3. Pack-Level Aggregation
docs.text:
Individual chunks are grouped into pack files to reduce the number of objects in the repository and improve I/O efficiency. Each pack file contains many chunks and is accompanied by an index that maps chunk hashes to offsets within the pack.

Together these layers mean that:

  • Identical files across different snapshots are stored only once.
  • Files that differ by a small amount share most of their chunks.
  • Backups of similar machines against the same repository benefit from cross-machine deduplication.

docs.title: S3 Backend Usage
docs.text:
HitStor supports Amazon S3 (and S3-compatible services) as a backend. The repository location is s3:<endpoint>/<bucket>: the repository uses the whole bucket. Include https:// in the endpoint; without a scheme HitStor connects over plain http://. To back up to an S3 bucket:

hitstor init --repo s3:https://s3.amazonaws.com/my-bucket --password "secret" \
    --s3-access-key AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE \
    --s3-secret-key wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY \
    --s3-region us-east-1

Then run backups against the same repo URI:

hitstor backup --repo s3:https://s3.amazonaws.com/my-bucket \
    --password "secret" \
    --s3-access-key AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE \
    --s3-secret-key wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY \
    /data

Credentials are not read from the AWS environment variables or shared credentials file. Pass them with flags or set them in the configuration file:

Flag Config key Purpose --s3-access-key s3_access_key Access key --s3-secret-key s3_secret_key Secret key --s3-region s3_region Bucket region (default us-east-1)

For S3-compatible services (MinIO, Backblaze B2, Wasabi), point the URI to the appropriate endpoint:

hitstor init --repo s3:https://s3.us-west-001.backblazeb2.com/my-bucket \
    --password "secret" --s3-access-key KEY_ID --s3-secret-key APPLICATION_KEY

Tip

Store your repository path and credentials in the config file or environment variables so you do not have to type them on every command. See Configuration.

docs.title: Bare-metal restore
docs.text:
Guided disaster recovery rebuilds a host that already boots and already runs a registered agent. Bare-metal restore covers the case it cannot: a machine with a blank disk, where there is no OS to install an agent onto and no partition table for the restored files to land in.

HitStor drives Relax-and-Recover (ReaR) for the parts that are not about data. ReaR builds bootable rescue media, recreates the disk layout, and reinstalls the bootloader; HitStor restores the contents.

Linux only for now

Windows bare-metal recovery (WinPE media, NTFS security descriptors, bcdboot) arrives in a later release.

docs.title: Why the media has to be built in advance
docs.text:
A rescue image embeds the host's own kernel, its drivers, and its disk layout. It can only be produced on the machine it protects, while that machine is still running — which is exactly what you no longer have when you need it.

So building recovery media is a deliberate, scheduled task, not something a backup does for you. Rebuild it whenever a host's storage layout changes: a stale image recreates the old layout.

The image is cached on the server rather than fetched from the host on demand. A design that rebuilt the ISO at download time would need the source host online and spend several minutes doing it, which breaks the feature in the one scenario it exists for.

docs.title: Capturing what a bare-metal restore needs
docs.text:
File contents alone do not describe a bootable machine. Add --bare-metal to a backup to capture the rest:

hitstor backup /etc /home /var --bare-metal

That records two things beyond the usual file tree:

  • Extended attributes — on Linux, SELinux contexts, file capabilities and POSIX ACLs are all xattrs, so one mechanism covers all three. Without them an SELinux system restores to an unlabeled filesystem whose services refuse to start.
  • The system profile — partition table, filesystem UUIDs and labels, LVM, software RAID, /etc/fstab, and bootloader state. Stored as an encrypted blob referenced from the snapshot, so the backup describes the machine's shape and not only its contents. The layout can be reconstructed even if the rescue media is lost.

Capture is best-effort throughout. A missing tool leaves that section empty and records a warning rather than failing the backup.

docs.title: Checking a host can build media
docs.text:
Run this on the protected host:

sudo hitstor-agent bmr check

It reports everything standing between that host and a bootable image at once — ReaR and its version, supporting tools, privileges — rather than stopping at the first problem, and exits non-zero when the host is not ready, so it can gate a provisioning script.

The same readiness appears per-host under Disaster Recovery → Bare Metal in the dashboard.

docs.title: Building the media
docs.text:
From the dashboard, under Disaster Recovery → Bare Metal, press Build media on a host. The server asks that host's agent to run ReaR and streams the resulting ISO back, showing the build as it happens. When it finishes, the image is cached on the server and Download appears.

Or on the host itself:

sudo hitstor-agent bmr build-media --server backup.example.com:8420

Useful flags:

Flag Purpose --migration-mode Allow recovery onto dissimilar hardware or a VM (P2V). ReaR remaps devices and regenerates the initramfs with the drivers the new hardware needs. --copy PATH Embed an extra file in the rescue image — a corporate CA bundle, say, without which the agent cannot verify the server. --agent NAME Registered agent name to prefill at the rescue prompt, when it differs from the hostname. --force Build despite readiness blockers.

rear mkrescue reads every disk on the machine and takes several minutes, so run it at a time when the extra load is acceptable.

Store the ISO somewhere that survives losing the host it came from.

docs.title: What is not on the media
docs.text:
No credentials. The recovery token, and where needed the repository password, are typed in at recovery time.

This is deliberate. Removable media that carried a working key would be a repository-compromise vector, and an ISO that still works a year after it was built, sitting on a shelf, is exactly the risk a long-lived credential creates. The cost is that unattended recovery is not possible unless you opt into it.

docs.title: Recovering a machine
docs.text:
1. Download that host's ISO from the Bare Metal tab and boot the replacement hardware from it.
  2. Back in the dashboard, press Issue token for the host. The token appears once — copy it. It works a single time, only for that host, and expires after 24 hours by default. If it leaks before use, Revoke it.
  3. At the rescue console, confirm the server address and agent name, then type the token. ReaR recreates the disk layout, mounts the new root at /mnt/local, and the recovery agent announces itself to the server.
  4. Return to Guided recovery and start the restore with the announced host as the target. Nothing starts on its own: a bare-metal restore is confirmed by an operator, like any other.
  5. When the restore reaches a terminal state the recovery agent exits, ReaR installs the bootloader, and the machine can be rebooted into the restored system.

docs.title: How the rescue host is reached
docs.text:
Every other restore is server-initiated: the server already knows an agent's address and dials in. A machine that just booted off rescue media has whatever address DHCP handed it, which nobody has told the server about.

So the rescue system calls home — presenting its recovery token and current address — and the server then dials back over the ordinary restore path, unchanged. The rescue system generates its own listener token for that dial-back; the original agent's token is never disclosed and stays valid for when the restored OS boots.

The server must be able to reach the rescue host

The dial-back needs a direct route to the address the rescue host announces. That holds for the same-LAN and P2V cases this release supports. A rescue host behind aggressive NAT across a WAN is not yet supported; the restore fails at start with the address it tried, rather than hanging.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Method Path Description GET /api/bmr/hosts Per-host readiness and cached media POST /api/bmr/media/{agent}/build Start a build; returns an operation id GET /api/operations/{id}/events Build progress (SSE) GET /api/bmr/media/{agent}/download Download the cached ISO DELETE /api/bmr/media/{agent} Discard the cached ISO POST /api/bmr/prepare/{agent} Mint a recovery token (returned once) GET /api/bmr/tokens List outstanding tokens DELETE /api/bmr/tokens/{id} Revoke an unused token 
# Issue a token with a tighter window than the 24h default.
curl -sS -X POST "$SERVER/api/bmr/prepare/web-01" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"ttl_hours": 2}'

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
bmr check reports blockers. Install what it names. On most distributions that is rear plus an ISO writer (xorriso or genisoimage). The command must run as root: ReaR reads raw block devices.

The build fails with a ReaR error. The message carries ReaR's own diagnosis. A previously cached image is left untouched — a rebuild that fails does not cost you the media you already had.

The rescue host announces but the restore will not start. The server could not reach the address it announced. Check routing and firewalls between the two, and that the port the rescue agent listens on (8422 by default) is open.

The token is rejected. Tokens are single-use, expire, and are bound to one host. Issue a fresh one; the error says which of the three applied.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Disaster recovery — guided restore onto a booting host
  • Restore files — single-snapshot granular restore
  • Agents — install and register an agent

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: HitStor can be configured through CLI flags, environment variables, and a YAML configuration file. This page explains how these sources interact, how to manage the config file, and how to use the interactive setup wizard. For the full list of keys, see the Configuration Reference.

docs.title: Config File Location
docs.text:
When --config is not given, HitStor uses the first of these that exists and is readable:

  1. /etc/hitstor/config.yaml -- the system-wide file used by the server service, the packages, and the installers.
  2. ~/.config/hitstor/config.yaml -- the per-user file (%AppData%\hitstor\config.yaml on Windows).

If neither exists, the per-user path is used, and hitstor config init or hitstor config set creates it there. Pass --config <path> to use any other file; hitstor config path prints the file in use.

docs.title: Precedence
docs.text:
When the same setting is specified in multiple places, HitStor applies the following precedence (highest to lowest):

  1. CLI flags -- always win.
  2. Config file -- provides persistent defaults.
  3. Environment variables -- used when neither a flag nor the config file sets the value.
  4. Built-in defaults -- used when nothing else is specified.

For example, if the config file sets repo: /backups/local but you pass --repo /backups/remote on the command line, the CLI flag takes effect. A HITSTOR_REPO environment variable is only used when neither sets the repository.

The repository password has no config file key of its own. It is taken from --password, then HITSTOR_PASSWORD, then --password-file, then the password_file of the repository selected with --repo-name.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
The following environment variables are recognized by the hitstor CLI:

Variable Purpose Example HITSTOR_REPO Default repository location export HITSTOR_REPO=/path/to/repo HITSTOR_PASSWORD Repository password export HITSTOR_PASSWORD=secret

See Environment Variables for the variables read by the server and the agent.

Warning

Avoid setting HITSTOR_PASSWORD in shell profiles or scripts stored in version control. Prefer --password-file (or a repository's password_file) pointing to a file with strict permissions (e.g., chmod 600).

docs.title: Config Commands
docs.text: HitStor provides a set of subcommands for managing the configuration file without editing YAML by hand.

docs.title: config show
docs.text:
Display the current configuration:

hitstor config show
Config file: /home/user/.config/hitstor/config.yaml

Configured repositories (1):
  [0] default
      Type:           local
      Path:           /backups/local
      Password file:  /etc/hitstor/password.txt [exists, readable]

Server settings (from this file):
  (none customized in this file)

Legacy single-repo keys (for backward compatibility):
  exclude                  *.tmp, node_modules  config
  parallel                 4                    config

Sensitive values such as S3 keys are masked in the output. config show --json lists every key with its value and source.

docs.title: config set
docs.text:
Set a single configuration key:

hitstor config set repo /backups/local
hitstor config set parallel 4

Keys are flat names (repo, password_file, parallel, exclude, s3_region, serve_port, and so on); the command lists the valid keys when given an unknown one.

docs.title: config unset
docs.text:
Remove a configuration key:

hitstor config unset parallel

docs.title: config add
docs.text:
Append a value to a list-type key:

hitstor config add exclude "*.log"
hitstor config add exclude ".cache"

docs.title: config remove
docs.text:
Remove a value from a list-type key:

hitstor config remove exclude "*.log"

docs.title: config init
docs.text: Launch the interactive setup wizard (see below).

docs.title: config edit
docs.text:
Open the config file in your editor ($EDITOR, then $VISUAL, else vi):

hitstor config edit

docs.title: config path
docs.text:
Print the path to the config file:

hitstor config path
/home/user/.config/hitstor/config.yaml

docs.title: Interactive Setup Wizard
docs.text:
The config init command walks you through the essential settings interactively. It needs an interactive terminal:

hitstor config init
Welcome to HitStor configuration setup!

Backend type (local/s3) [local]:
Repository path: /backups/local
Password file (optional): /etc/hitstor/password.txt
Parallel workers (0 = auto) [0]: 4
Exclude patterns (comma-separated, optional): *.tmp, node_modules

Configuration saved to /home/user/.config/hitstor/config.yaml

For s3 it asks for the repository (s3:endpoint/bucket), the S3 access key, secret key, and region instead of a path. If a config file already exists, the wizard asks before overwriting it and offers the current values as defaults.

docs.title: Local Repository
docs.text:
A minimal config for backing up to a local disk:

repo: /mnt/external/hitstor-repo
password_file: /etc/hitstor/password.txt
parallel: 4
exclude:
  - "*.tmp"
  - ".cache"
  - "node_modules"

When both repo and password_file are set, HitStor treats them as a repository named default. Select it with --repo-name default so the password is read from the file, or pass --password-file yourself:

hitstor --repo-name default backup /data

docs.title: S3 Repository
docs.text:
Backing up to an S3-compatible bucket:

repo: s3:https://s3.amazonaws.com/my-bucket
s3_access_key: AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE
s3_secret_key: wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY
s3_region: us-east-1
parallel: 8
exclude:
  - "*.tmp"
  - ".cache"

The repository uses the whole bucket. S3 credentials come from the s3_* keys or the --s3-access-key, --s3-secret-key, and --s3-region flags; the AWS environment variables and shared credentials file are not read. Give the repository password with --password-file or HITSTOR_PASSWORD.

docs.title: Remote Agent Setup
docs.text:
The agent (hitstor-agent) reads agent_* keys. A dashboard-managed agent needs none of them: registration stores the server address and API key in agent.env. For an agent registered by hand:

agent_server: backup.example.com:8420
agent_api_key: a1b2c3d4...   # 64-char hex, from `hitstor serve agent add <name>`
agent_ca_cert: /etc/hitstor/ca.pem
agent_hostname: webserver-01
agent_paths:
  - /etc
  - /var/www
agent_excludes:
  - "*.tmp"

On the server, alert_notifier_plugins and alert_webhook_url configure alert delivery; see Plugins.

docs.title: Sensitive Values
docs.text:
HitStor takes care not to expose sensitive configuration values:

  • config show masks secrets such as S3 keys.
  • The config file itself is not encrypted, except for values the server stores encrypted with the repository key (for example the S3 keys of repositories created from the dashboard, and email and integration secrets). Protect it with appropriate file-system permissions (chmod 600 ~/.config/hitstor/config.yaml).
  • Prefer password_file (or --password-file) over passing the password on the command line. The file should also have strict permissions.

Tip

You can combine the config file with environment variables for a layered approach: store non-sensitive defaults in the config file and inject the password through HITSTOR_PASSWORD at runtime.

docs.title: Disaster recovery (guided full-system restore)
docs.text: HitStor protects filesystems, not raw disks. Disaster recovery means rebuilding a host from its file backups onto new or repaired hardware with a guided dashboard wizard.

docs.title: What this is (and is not)
docs.text:
Is Is not Full restore of all file backup jobs for a system Block-level disk imaging Sequential restore of each job’s latest snapshot Automatic OS reinstall / bootloader repair Staging root or original-path modes Hypervisor VM import

After the OS and HitStor agent are installed on the recovery host, the wizard restores application and data paths from the repository.

Workload jobs, such as SQL Server databases, are not part of the plan: once the host and its database engine are back, restore them with the plugin restore.

For a machine with a blank disk — no OS to install an agent onto, no partition table to restore into — see Bare-metal restore, which recreates the disk layout and bootloader first and then hands the data restore back to this wizard.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
1. Recovery host has a compatible OS (Windows or Linux).
  2. HitStor agent installed and registered with the backup server.
  3. Enough free disk for the data (or a large staging volume).
  4. Source system’s backup jobs have completed at least once (snapshots present).

Optional but recommended: jobs with restore verification green (see Backups page).

docs.title: Dashboard wizard
docs.text:
Open Disaster Recovery in the sidebar (/disaster).

  1. Select system — protected agent (source) with jobs/snapshots.
  2. Review plan — each job’s latest snapshot, paths, size, last verify status.
  3. Target agent — usually the new host; can be the same agent after rebuild.
  4. Mode
  5. Staging root (default): restore under e.g. /recover/hostname/job-name for review, then cut over.
  6. Original paths: write to live paths (stop services that lock files first).
  7. Start full-system recovery — restores run one job after another on the target agent.

Progress appears on the same page (and under Restores for individual sessions).

docs.title: API (operators / automation)
docs.text:
Method Path Description GET /api/disaster/plans Summary of systems and readiness GET /api/disaster/plans/{agent} Full plan + checklist POST /api/disaster/recover Start recovery GET /api/disaster/recoveries List orchestrated recoveries GET /api/disaster/recoveries/{id} One recovery status

These endpoints need the session cookie of a signed-in user: reading plans and recoveries needs a role on every agent, and starting a recovery needs an administrator with a recent sign-in (see Dashboard HTTP API). Example:

curl -sS -X POST "$SERVER/api/disaster/recover" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "source_agent": "web-01",
    "target_agent": "web-01-new",
    "mode": "staging",
    "staging_root": "/recover/web-01"
  }'

docs.title: After recovery
docs.text:
1. Validate application data under staging (or live paths).
  2. Cut over DNS/services as needed.
  3. Re-point or recreate backup jobs on the recovery agent.
  4. Optionally run hitstor verify-restore <snapshot> for an extra integrity check.
